firstQualityStart.thirdNumberTitle: A third always has the number 3
firstQualityStart.thirdNumberBody: Before naming a $t(glossary:third_one) more precisely, check its number: three letter-name positions including start and destination. A–B–C forms a third, as do E–F–G and F–G–A. Now add a second property: distance in half steps. Thirds on natural notes, as used in this unit, span three or four half steps. The extra name is the $t(glossary:intervalQuality_one). Number and quality together make the full interval name.
firstQualityStart.minorBody: A minor third combines interval number 3 with three half steps. For E4–G4, the letter-name positions E–F–G number three. On the keyboard, the moves E–F–F-sharp–G also give three half steps, starting at 0. The answer is “minor third”. A descending minor third still spans three half steps; read its direction from the notation. Note duration does not determine quality.
firstQualityStart.majorBody: A major third still has number 3 but spans four half steps. F–G–A occupies three letter-name positions; F–F-sharp–G–G-sharp–A spans four key moves. G–B is also a major third of four half steps. Two thirds therefore need not look differently spaced on the staff. After counting letter-name positions, check sounding distance. This unit uses natural notes in the treble clef only.
firstQualityStart.perfectBody: A perfect fourth combines number 4 with five half steps; a perfect fifth combines number 5 with seven. E–F–G–A occupies four letter-name positions: E4–A4 is a perfect fourth spanning five half steps. E–F–G–A–B occupies five: E4–B4 is a perfect fifth spanning seven. “Perfect” is the quality name for these intervals. Both number and half-step distance must fit; the number of positions alone is not enough.
firstQualityStart.octaveBody: A perfect $t(glossary:octave_one) repeats a letter name in the next octave register. E–F–G–A–B–C–D–E occupies eight letter-name positions and spans twelve half steps. E4–E5 is therefore a perfect octave. Reversing the order keeps the twelve-half-step distance and makes the pattern descending. Distinguish equal letter names in different registers from a repeated pitch with distance 0.
firstQualityStart.tritoneBody: A $t(glossary:tritone_one) spans three whole steps, or six half steps; strictly, this means F–B. F–B has interval number 4 but six half steps instead of five; it is not a perfect fourth. B to F in the next register has number 5 but six half steps instead of seven; it is not a perfect fifth. B–F spans the same number of $t(glossary:semitone_other) as F–B and is often also called a tritone. Answer “No” for both when checking perfect intervals. The two notations share a half-step distance but have different interval numbers. Their other quality names come later.
firstQualityStart.zeroCaption: G4–G4: the same key again, 0 moves.
firstQualityStart.minorCaption: E4–G4: number 3 and 3 half steps, minor third.
firstQualityStart.majorCaption: F4–A4: number 3 and 4 half steps, major third.
firstQualityStart.majorOtherCaption: G4–B4: also a major third with 4 half steps.
firstQualityStart.fourthCaption: E4–A4: number 4 and 5 half steps, perfect fourth.
firstQualityStart.fifthCaption: E4–B4: number 5 and 7 half steps, perfect fifth.
firstQualityStart.octaveCaption: E4–E5: number 8 and 12 half steps, perfect octave.
firstQualityStart.tritoneFourthCaption: F4–B4: number 4 and 6 half steps, not a perfect fourth.
firstQualityStart.tritoneFifthCaption: B4–F5: number 5 and 6 half steps, not a perfect fifth.

auralRhythmStart.card1Body: The $t(glossary:pulse) provides a regular sense of time. Listen to the higher starting sounds and the evenly spaced clicks that follow. All beats between two beginnings belong to one group; the next beginning belongs to the next group. You can quietly count or move along. Here, clicks deliberately make the pulse clear.
auralRhythmStart.card1Example1: Two beats per group, heard twice.
auralRhythmStart.card1Example2: Three beats per group, heard twice.
auralRhythmStart.card2Body: The $t(glossary:rhythm_one) can contain several starts within a pulse beat and silent passages. The pulse continues as a reference. Listen first to the steady sequence, then to the example with shorter sounds. A new note start is not automatically a new pulse beat. This unit begins with simple quarter-note and eighth-note patterns.
auralRhythmStart.card2Example2: Two short sounds share the first quarter-note beat.
auralRhythmStart.card3Title: Do not count the next beginning twice
auralRhythmStart.card3Body: When listening to two groups, start counting at the higher click with 1. In a four-beat group, 2, 3 and 4 follow. The next higher click begins again at 1. Loudness and pitch help identify the beginning here; this does not imply that every musical beginning must sound higher.
auralRhythmStart.card4Title: Compare two rhythms using the same rule
auralRhythmStart.card4Body: You hear example A, a short separating gap and example B. Here, “same” means the same note starts, durations and rests at the same tempo. Both examples use the same piano pitch so that pitch does not distract from rhythm. Listen to both in full and start again from the beginning when replaying.
auralRhythmStart.card4Example1: A: the second beat is divided.
auralRhythmStart.card4Example2: B: the same starts and durations as A.
auralRhythmStart.card5Body: Two examples can have the same number of note starts and still have different rhythms. Compare which beat contains the short sounds. In the first example, the first beat is divided; in the second, the second beat is divided. Both measures have the same total length. Simply counting notes is therefore insufficient.
auralRhythmStart.card5Example1: A: two eighth notes at the beginning.
auralRhythmStart.card5Example2: B: two eighth notes after the first quarter note.
auralRhythmStart.card6Title: Rests are part of the comparison
auralRhythmStart.card6Body: A $t(glossary:rest_one) is a notated silent span. It does not end the measure. Keep listening until the next note start and maintain the pulse internally. Replacing a note with a rest changes the audible rhythm even when the total measure length stays the same. The separating gap between A and B is not part of either example measure.
auralRhythmStart.card6Example1: A quarter rest on the third beat.
auralRhythmStart.card6Example2: A quarter note sounds at that point instead.
auralRhythmStart.card7Title: Match a heard rhythm to notation
auralRhythmStart.card7Body: In the selection question, you hear exactly one complete measure. The three numbered scores show different rhythms on the same pitch. Read their beginnings and find the first point where they differ. Then match the heard starts, durations and rests. A score number does not indicate whether it is correct.
auralRhythmStart.card7Example1: The third quarter-note beat consists of two eighth notes.
auralRhythmStart.card8Body: A $t(glossary:notes.quarter_one) lasts one pulse beat here; two $t(glossary:notes.eighth_other) divide it equally. A sound can continue without a new start. Listen to both starts and duration. All scores form the same complete four-four measure; their events must add up to the measure length.
auralRhythmStart.card8Example1: Quarter note, two eighth notes, quarter note, quarter note.
auralRhythmStart.card9Title: Find silence in the matching score
auralRhythmStart.card9Body: When you hear a short gap, look for the corresponding rest in the score. Do not confuse a note ending without a new start with an additional note. The examples begin with a note and contain no accidentals or dots. You can replay freely; unavailable audio is recorded as skipped listening work.
auralRhythmStart.card9Example1: An eighth rest follows the first quarter note.
auralRhythmStart.lesson3: Match a heard rhythm to its score

auralPitchStart.articleTitle: Pitch direction, melodies and first listening intervals
auralPitchStart.card1Body: Compare the second sound with the first. For “higher”, sounding pitch increases. The second sound need not be louder or longer. Listen to the pitches in sequence; the question asks for no note names and requires no absolute pitch. Direction will later be linked to interval names.
auralPitchStart.card2Body: For “lower”, sounding pitch decreases. Do not equate a quieter sound with a lower pitch. In the example, A4 is followed by F4; the second lies lower. The score stays hidden before checking in listening questions so that the answer is based on hearing.
auralPitchStart.card3Body: A repeated pitch has two separate starts at the same pitch. It is not one long sound. For “same pitch”, compare height rather than the number of starts. Both sounds use the same piano timbre in these questions, keeping the focus on direction and repetition.
auralPitchStart.card4Body: For melody comparisons, you hear four pitches in A and then four in B. “Same” means the same sounding pitches in the same order with the same durations. A similar contour or transposed sequence is not “same” here. Both examples stay short and use natural notes so you can follow each pitch mentally.
auralPitchStart.card5Body: Two melodies can begin and end on the same pitch while a middle pitch differs. Compare each position in order. In these examples, only the second pitch changes; durations remain the same. One difference is enough for “different”. You do not need to name every note.
auralPitchStart.card5Example1: A has G4 in the second position.
auralPitchStart.card6Body: Hear the first melody as a short unit, then compare the beginning, middle and end of the second. Tempo and timbre stay the same within a question; pitch and timing are the assessed properties. The gap helps orientation and is not part of the melody. Replaying supports learning without creating a new question.
auralPitchStart.card6Example1: Beginning G4, middle E4–F4, ending G4.
auralPitchStart.card7Title: Hear ascending minor and major thirds
auralPitchStart.card7Body: A minor third spans three $t(glossary:semitone_other); a major third spans four. Both are $t(glossary:third_other); by ear, their sounding distances differ. Here, the starting pitch is followed by the higher destination. Compare the two original examples without relying on song openings as fixed mnemonics. The introductory score provides a check.
auralPitchStart.card8Title: Hear ascending perfect fourths and fifths
auralPitchStart.card8Body: A perfect fourth spans five $t(glossary:semitone_other); a perfect fifth spans seven. These questions play pitches in ascending sequence rather than simultaneously. Compare the distance from the first pitch. The example can start in a different register; the interval name depends on the relationship, not an absolute note name.
auralPitchStart.card9Body: Finally, minor third, major third, perfect fourth and perfect fifth are offered together. Hear the starting pitch and then the distance. All questions remain ascending and use natural notes. Further qualities, descending listening intervals and longer melodies belong to the next level. An error review uses a new sound rather than only rearranged buttons.
auralPitchStart.card9Example1: G4–B4: a major third from a different starting pitch.
auralPitchStart.lesson1: Hear higher, lower and repeated pitches
auralPitchStart.lesson3: Hear ascending thirds, fourths and fifths

historySourcesStart.articleTitle: Sound sources, documents and musical context
historySourcesStart.card1Body: A $t(glossary:voice_one) is produced in singing by vibrating vocal folds. An $t(glossary:instrument_one) uses a vibrating string, membrane or air column, for example. Electronic devices can generate audio signals. These describe production rather than mutually exclusive labels for an entire recording: one performance can combine several sound sources.
historySourcesStart.card1Example1: The model plays piano pitches and does not reproduce a singing voice. Original piano teaching model.
historySourcesStart.card2Title: A recording is a playback medium
historySourcesStart.card2Body: A $t(glossary:recording_one) stores sound for later playback. It can contain voices, instruments and electronic sounds together. A loudspeaker reproduces the stored signal; it alone does not establish how the original sound was produced. Distinguish production from playback. Our sound examples are original piano teaching models rather than historical performances.
historySourcesStart.card2Example1: The written score is played as a piano model here. Original piano teaching model.
historySourcesStart.card3Body: “Singing with piano accompaniment” identifies a voice and an instrument. “A recording of it” adds the medium without replacing those sources. A choir consists of several singers; a choir recording is both vocal sound and stored playback. You should not guess human voices or instrument identities from our piano models. The questions ask about unambiguous descriptions of these terms.
historySourcesStart.card3Example1: A single written melody does not by itself establish choir forces. Original piano teaching model.
historySourcesStart.card4Title: Distinguish a score from a performance
historySourcesStart.card4Body: A $t(glossary:scoreSource_one) uses symbols to specify pitches, durations and further instructions. It does not itself sound. A performance realizes those instructions through decisions about tempo, timbre and shaping. Our displayed teaching score and playback intentionally match exactly; historical sources require separate consideration of edition, transmission and interpretation.
historySourcesStart.card4Example1: Written instructions and their sounding realization. Original piano teaching model.
historySourcesStart.card5Body: A recording lets you hear particular starts, sound shapes and interpretative choices. It does not automatically prove identical notation or a correct label. Editing, splicing and playback technology can affect the result. Check recording date, performers and provenance separately. This teaching model demonstrates only its own played score.
historySourcesStart.card5Example1: An audible rest is an observation about this model. Original piano teaching model.
historySourcesStart.card6Body: A $t(glossary:report_one) describes an event from one perspective. A $t(glossary:programmeSource_one) announces a work, performers, place and date, for example. An announcement alone does not prove that everything occurred; a report can be mistaken. Compare sources and distinguish their claims. Fictional teaching information is explicitly labeled and does not replace historical evidence.
historySourcesStart.card6Example1: Fictional program: “Piano teaching model, town hall, 2026”. Original piano teaching model.
historySourcesStart.card7Body: The $t(glossary:place_one) asks where a performance happened. Sources may name a church, concert hall or private room. A short piano sound alone does not establish a performance venue. The example’s fictional program says “town hall”: that is place information, not a listening observation. Real history requires checkable provenance and sources.
historySourcesStart.card7Example1: Fictional teaching information: venue town hall. Original piano teaching model.
historySourcesStart.card8Title: Date composition, performance and recording separately
historySourcesStart.card8Body: The $t(glossary:time_one) asks when a particular event occurred. A work’s composition, a later performance and a still later recording can have different dates. Identify which date a source refers to. “2026” in the fictional teaching program is an event date; it does not date a historical composition. A familiar sound style does not replace this evidence.
historySourcesStart.card8Example1: Fictional teaching information: event date 2026. Original piano teaching model.
historySourcesStart.card9Body: The $t(glossary:occasion_one) names the event, such as a wedding or benefit concert. $t(glossary:author) asks who wrote the music or report. Performers, composers and reporters can be different people. In the fictional example, “benefit concert” is the occasion. These categories help read sources purposefully and identify unsupported guesses.
historySourcesStart.card9Example1: Fictional teaching information: occasion benefit concert. Original piano teaching model.
historySourcesStart.lesson3: Identify place, time and occasion in a source

historyOverviewStart.articleTitle: Periods, performing forces and supported listening observations
historyOverviewStart.card1Title: A broad sequence of European periods
historyOverviewStart.card1Body: This introduction covers European art music rather than the entire history of world music. The conventional broad sequence is Middle Ages, Renaissance, Baroque, Classical period, Romantic period and music since 1900. It supports orientation in time and does not rank styles as better. Ordering questions ask for this sequence. The piano model is not a historical style sample and cannot be dated from it.
historyOverviewStart.card1Example1: A simple-sounding melody does not establish a medieval date. Original piano teaching model.
historyOverviewStart.card2Title: Approximate dates rather than rigid boundaries
historyOverviewStart.card2Body: For learning orientation, we use roughly 500–1400 for the Middle Ages, 1400–1600 for the Renaissance and 1600–1750 for the Baroque. For the Classical period, roughly 1750–1820; for Romanticism, mainly the nineteenth century. Boundaries vary by region and topic; Classical and Romantic periods overlap. The sequence is an overview, not an automatic way to date music.
historyOverviewStart.card2Example1: A piano model alone provides no evidence for a period. Original piano teaching model.
historyOverviewStart.card3Body: “Music since 1900” groups the twentieth and twenty-first centuries here. It is not a single style. Earlier music also continues to be performed and newly recorded. Composition date and the date of a heard recording remain separate questions. Period terms help organize information; detailed work histories and further musical traditions are explored later.
historyOverviewStart.card3Example1: A present-day teaching model can use the same pitches as earlier music. Original piano teaching model.
historyOverviewStart.card4Title: Genre names a kind of work
historyOverviewStart.card4Body: A $t(glossary:genre_one) describes a kind of work. In this introduction, an opera combines mostly sung music with staged action; a symphony is typically a multi-movement orchestral composition. These short descriptions do not replace the history of their varied forms. Genre does not establish the specific event where a work was performed. A short melody alone does not reliably identify an opera or symphony.
historyOverviewStart.card4Example1: Four notes do not establish a genre. Original piano teaching model.
historyOverviewStart.card5Body: The $t(glossary:performingForces_one) describes participating voices and instruments. A choir consists of several singers; an orchestra of several instrumental performers. A string quartet normally uses two violins, viola and cello. Children’s, men’s and women’s choirs are descriptions of forces; a single pitch does not establish these forces. Genre and forces answer different questions.
historyOverviewStart.card5Example1: Two piano pitches are not a recording of a choir or string quartet. Original piano teaching model.
historyOverviewStart.card6Title: Occasion and function are different questions
historyOverviewStart.card6Body: Occasion names the specific event, such as a wedding ceremony. $t(glossary:function_one) asks what purpose music served there: dancing, worship or focused listening, for example. The same work can serve different purposes in different contexts. Performing forces are therefore neither a function nor automatically a genre. Read carefully which question is described in an exercise.
historyOverviewStart.card6Example1: Sound alone establishes neither a wedding nor a dance function. Original piano teaching model.
historyOverviewStart.card7Title: Call only what is heard an observation
historyOverviewStart.card7Body: A $t(glossary:observation_one) describes directly checkable sound. “Two pitches sound together” can be heard in the example. “The piece originated in a church in 1750” includes date and place claims for which the example alone provides no evidence. Our models contain either pitches sounding only in sequence or at least one joint start of two pitches.
historyOverviewStart.card7Example1: One pitch, silence, then another pitch. Original piano teaching model.
historyOverviewStart.card7Example2: Two pitches begin together. Original piano teaching model.
historyOverviewStart.card8Body: $t(glossary:sourceInformation_one) may give place, date or authorship. An $t(glossary:inference_one) combines observations and checked information into an informed conclusion. Neither sound similarity nor an unchecked label alone establishes certainty. Identify the source of a statement and distinguish it from what you directly heard. The exercise asks for the directly audible statement about the original model.
historyOverviewStart.card8Example1: The pitches and rest are audible; no historical date is given. Original piano teaching model.
historyOverviewStart.card9Body: When evidence is missing or contradictory, $t(glossary:uncertainty) is an accurate description. You do not need to guess a venue or period. Check whether a statement is supported by hearing or an appropriate source. Starts and simultaneous pitches can be checked in the original piano model; historical provenance is not claimed. This keeps observation precise and history connected to sources.
historyOverviewStart.card9Example1: A joint start does not establish historical provenance. Original piano teaching model.

clefsStart.articleTitle: Bass clef, grand staff and octave names
clefsStart.anchorBody: The two dots of the $t(glossary:bassClef_one) surround the fourth line from the bottom. That line is f, or F3 scientifically. This is why it is also called the F clef. Count lines from the bottom; the same position has a different name in another clef.
clefsStart.ladderTitle: Step by step from c to b
clefsStart.ladderBody: Moving from a line to the next space is one letter-name step. In the $t(glossary:bassClef_one), c/C3 occupies the second space from the bottom. Above it come d, e, f, g, a, b. The third, fourth and fifth lines hold d, f and a; e and g lie between them, and b lies just above the top line. Use reference notes and count in either direction.
clefsStart.middleBody: After b/B3, c¹/C4 starts the next $t(glossary:octaveRegister_one). This middle C occupies the first $t(glossary:ledgerLine_one) above the bass staff. The short line belongs to the note. c and c¹ share their letter name but are an octave apart. Include the register in the final four questions.
clefsStart.pairBody: The $t(glossary:grandStaff_one) connects an upper staff in the $t(glossary:trebleClef_one) with a lower staff in the $t(glossary:bassClef_one). The connection groups them together; each clef retains its own pitch mapping. Two staves do not imply exactly two voices or a compulsory division between hands. Here only one contains a note; the other has a whole-measure rest.
clefsStart.sharedBody: c¹/C4 occupies the first $t(glossary:ledgerLine_one) below the upper staff in the $t(glossary:trebleClef_one). The same pitch lies on the first above the lower staff in the $t(glossary:bassClef_one). The examples show these spellings separately: both sound the same and mark the same key. Their available pitch ranges overlap; a note on the lower staff is not automatically lower than every note on the upper one.
clefsStart.findTitle: From staff to the right key
clefsStart.findBody: Read the clef of the staff containing the note first. Then identify its letter name and $t(glossary:octaveRegister_one) before choosing a key. Here you practise a/A3 through e¹/E4, with the keyboard fixed to that range. b/B3 is the white key immediately left of c¹/C4. A rest on the other staff adds no second target pitch.
clefsStart.helmBody: The $t(glossary:helmholtzNotation) uses case and superscripts: C is great C (C2), c is small c (C3), c¹ is one-line c (C4), and c² is two-line c (C5). The same register marking applies to all seven letter names: c–b, then c¹–b¹. Our exercises start at C3; the card also shows C2 for comparison.
clefsStart.scienceBody: In $t(glossary:scientificNotation), a number follows the international uppercase letter: C3–B3, then C4–B4. Middle C is C4. The number changes at C, not at A. Switching naming systems preserves the pitch. Translate Helmholtz to scientific notation in the first half, then in the opposite direction.
clefsStart.lettersBody: This lesson always uses international scientific names: German h = B3 and German h¹ = B4. German B would be a lowered H, international B♭; it is absent from these natural-note tasks. Check both the letter-name system and the register when translating. The right letter in the wrong octave is an incorrect answer.
clefsStart.sharedExample1: c¹ = C4 in the treble clef
clefsStart.sharedExample2: c¹ = C4 in the bass clef: the same key
clefsStart.scienceExample1: B3 → C4: the number increases at C
clefsStart.lettersExample1: German h, international b; scientifically B3

levelTwoSpelling.articleTitle: Accidentals, enharmonic spelling and note writing
levelTwoSpelling.scopeBody: An $t(glossary:accidental_one) before a note applies to later notes of the same letter in the same octave until the next barline. In this example F-sharp repeats in the same measure without a second sharp. Read clef, measure and register together.
levelTwoSpelling.scopeCaption: F-sharp twice; the second sharp is not printed again
levelTwoSpelling.resetBody: At the $t(glossary:barline_one), an individual accidental’s scope ends. The $t(glossary:keySignature_one) applies again. With no key signature, F-sharp in the first measure becomes F in the next. A tie specially continues the same pitch; the rhythm unit covers that case.
levelTwoSpelling.resetCaption: F-sharp before the barline, F afterwards
levelTwoSpelling.naturalBody: A $t(glossary:natural_one) cancels the alteration previously in force for this letter in this register. In our reading model, an accidental on F4 does not automatically affect F5. Key signatures apply to their letter names in every octave. These tasks use single accidentals.
levelTwoSpelling.naturalCaption: F-sharp, cancelled F, F-sharp, and F in the next octave
levelTwoSpelling.enharmonicTitle: C-sharp and D-flat share a key
levelTwoSpelling.enharmonicBody: With $t(glossary:enharmonic), differently written pitches can sound alike. C-sharp raises C; D-flat lowers D. On an equal-tempered piano both reach the same key. Their written letters remain different and matter for intervals and chords.
levelTwoSpelling.enharmonicCaption: C-sharp and D-flat: same key, different letter positions
levelTwoSpelling.edgesTitle: Even without an intervening black key
levelTwoSpelling.edgesBody: E–F and B–C already span one $t(glossary:semitone_one). E-sharp therefore sounds like F, and B-sharp like the next C. An alteration belongs to the written letter, rather than a key colour. B-sharp can have a different scientific octave number from its equivalent C.
levelTwoSpelling.spellingTitle: Sound equivalence does not preserve notation
levelTwoSpelling.spellingBody: Finding a key requires the correct sounding pitch. Writing a note also requires its letter, alteration and octave. D-flat therefore does not correctly spell a requested C-sharp, even though they sound alike. Check whether each task asks about sound or spelling.
levelTwoSpelling.spellingCaption: Two sounding equivalents followed by natural C
levelTwoSpelling.writeBody: When writing, place the $t(glossary:notehead_one) on the correct letter-name position, then choose the single accidental. The task names a full pitch: C4 is a different register from C3. Check the clef before moving the notehead.
levelTwoSpelling.writeCaption: D4 and D-sharp4 keep the same letter position
levelTwoSpelling.bassTitle: The bass clef keeps its mapping
levelTwoSpelling.bassBody: In the $t(glossary:bassClef_one), C4 occupies the first ledger line above the staff. C-sharp retains that notehead position and adds a sharp. In treble clef this pitch lies below the staff. Sound follows pitch; position follows clef.
levelTwoSpelling.bassCaption: C4 and C-sharp4 in bass clef
levelTwoSpelling.checkBody: Check letter name, accidental and register in that order. Writing controls change these properties separately. The first evaluation locks the answer; an error review uses a new pitch. Enharmonic replacements count as errors in these writing tasks.
levelTwoSpelling.checkCaption: B-flat3 and B3 in the same register

levelTwoDottedTied.dotBody: A dot extends a note value by half its original value. A dotted quarter equals quarter plus eighth: 1 + 1/2 = 3/2 quarter-note values. This is a duration, rather than a new meter. This unit uses exactly one dot.
levelTwoDottedTied.dotCaption: Dotted quarter plus eighth equals two quarters
levelTwoDottedTied.eighthBody: A dotted eighth equals eighth plus sixteenth. Together with another sixteenth it fills one quarter-note value. The two onsets divide that span unequally: three sixteenths to one. First count equal small subdivisions.
levelTwoDottedTied.fractionBody: A dotted half lasts three quarter-note values. A dotted eighth instead lasts three quarters of one quarter-note value. A number needs a reference unit. These tasks explicitly measure duration in quarter-note values.
levelTwoDottedTied.tieBody: A $t(glossary:tie) connects consecutive notes of the same written pitch. The second note has no new onset; durations are added. Connecting different pitches is not a tie. A phrase or slur marking has a different function.
levelTwoDottedTied.tieCaption: Two tied quarters: one sound across two beats
levelTwoDottedTied.chainBody: Three or more identical notes can form a tie chain. Read through the first note without a further tie. Rests do not belong to that chain. Here G has one onset and lasts three quarter-note values; the following rest is silent.
levelTwoDottedTied.compareTitle: Compare a dot and a tie
levelTwoDottedTied.compareBody: A dotted quarter and a tied quarter plus eighth have the same total duration. The second spelling makes a subdivision clearer. Compare duration while retaining the written structure. Here each of the two pitches lasts one and a half quarter-note values.
levelTwoDottedTied.compareCaption: Dotted G; A tied for the same duration
levelTwoDottedTied.crossbarBody: A $t(glossary:barline_one) does not end a tie. The pitch continues into the next measure without a new onset there. Its alteration also carries through the tie. Add the note values on both sides to find total duration.
levelTwoDottedTied.crossbarCaption: F-sharp starts before the barline and continues afterwards
levelTwoDottedTied.syncopationBody: In this simple $t(glossary:syncopation_one), a pitch starts between beats and continues across the following beat, bridging a normally stronger position. A short offbeat eighth alone does not meet this task’s criterion. Listen for the uninterrupted duration.
levelTwoDottedTied.syncopationCaption: Onset on the second eighth, held across the next quarter beat
levelTwoDottedTied.countBody: Keep counting beats evenly even when no new note starts. A tie adds no onset. Later tapping tasks count actual onsets only. Compare the syncopation with this sequence whose note starts fall on beats.

levelTwoSubdivision.threeTitle: Three in the time of two
levelTwoSubdivision.threeBody: A $t(glossary:triplet_one) divides the time of two equal notes into three equal parts. Three triplet eighths together last as long as two ordinary eighths: one quarter. The number 3 labels the group rather than the meter.
levelTwoSubdivision.threeCaption: Three triplet eighths within one quarter
levelTwoSubdivision.equalBody: The three triplet parts have equal duration. This is neither a dotted long-short rhythm nor an unequal swing instruction. Count three evenly spaced syllables per quarter-note beat. The task checks all three actual onsets.
levelTwoSubdivision.equalCaption: Two quarter beats, each divided into three
levelTwoSubdivision.tapBody: Before tapping, hear a complete count-in measure. Then enter each written note onset. Each three-eighth triplet fills exactly one beat. The fourth onset begins the next group of three; avoid adding a pause between groups.
levelTwoSubdivision.tapCaption: Nine onsets within three quarter-note beats
levelTwoSubdivision.simpleBody: Simple 3/4 has three quarter-note beats. Each normally divides into two eighths. Six eighth notes fill the measure, grouped 2 + 2 + 2. The meter and beam groups show that organization.
levelTwoSubdivision.compoundBody: Compound 6/8 normally groups its six eighths as 3 + 3. Its two beats each have the value of a dotted quarter. The numerator 6 does not imply six ordinary beats here. Read the eighths as subdivisions within the two groups.
levelTwoSubdivision.sameTotalBody: At the same eighth-note duration, 3/4 and 6/8 have equal total length. Their usual grouping differs: three pairs versus two triples. The denominator alone does not always describe the musical beat. These tasks ask about beat count and beat value together.
levelTwoSubdivision.groupBody: The $t(glossary:beam_other) group eighths by the two beats in 6/8. Group one starts on eighth 1; group two starts on eighth 4. Count each beat with three even subdivisions. Actual onsets may occupy only some of those positions.
levelTwoSubdivision.groupCaption: Quarter plus eighth, then eighth plus quarter
levelTwoSubdivision.restsBody: A rest has the same duration as the corresponding note value. It places the following note on its proper subdivision. Do not tap a rest, but continue counting internally. These tasks use the dotted quarter as the count-in beat.
levelTwoSubdivision.distinguishBody: Three ordinary eighths already form one beat in 6/8, so no triplet number is required. Three eighths under a 3 within a quarter-note beat are instead a triplet. Both have three parts but different reference units; always check the meter.
levelTwoSubdivision.distinguishCaption: Ordinary eighths in 6/8, without a triplet number

levelTwoQualitiesBuild.numberBody: The $t(glossary:intervalQuality_one) requires both letter-name distance and semitone distance. Include both endpoints when counting the number. C–E is a third; C–F is a fourth. Then check sounding steps. A semitone count alone does not determine an interval’s full spelling.
levelTwoQualitiesBuild.familiesBody: Unison, fourth, fifth and octave belong to the perfect classes. Second, third, sixth and seventh initially distinguish minor and major. Augmented and diminished alterations are possible in both families. This stage covers simple intervals through the octave.
levelTwoQualitiesBuild.familiesCaption: Perfect fourth: four letter names, five semitones
levelTwoQualitiesBuild.qualitiesTitle: Altering a pitch preserves its letter
levelTwoQualitiesBuild.qualitiesBody: An accidental changes sounding distance without changing letter position. C–E is major and C–E-flat minor; both remain thirds. C–F-sharp is an augmented fourth. Comparing with a perfect or major reference helps naming, but does not replace counting.
levelTwoQualitiesBuild.buildNumberBody: To build a major third from C, count C as 1, D as 2 and E as 3. This fixes the target letter E. Then determine its alteration. The writing task preserves the starting pitch and asks for the complete second pitch.
levelTwoQualitiesBuild.buildQualityBody: A minor third from D needs F: three semitones. A major third from D needs F-sharp: four. Both use the letter F. Add an accidental when the requested quality requires it, and retain the correct octave.
levelTwoQualitiesBuild.buildCheckBody: Check the counted letters first, then the semitone count. An enharmonically equivalent key with the wrong letter does not meet the writing task. The exact written pitch, including alteration and octave, matters here. The display uses German or English note names.
levelTwoQualitiesBuild.tritoneBody: C–F-sharp and C–G-flat sound alike on an equal-tempered piano. The first spans four letters and is an augmented fourth; the second spans five and is a diminished fifth. Both are tritone distances. Visual tasks can distinguish these spellings; purely aural tasks cannot.
levelTwoQualitiesBuild.thirdFourthTitle: Four semitones can also be ambiguous
levelTwoQualitiesBuild.thirdFourthBody: C–E is a major third. C–F-flat sounds the same but is a diminished fourth. The flat lowers a perfect fourth by one semitone. Its number remains a fourth because the letter is F. Sounding distance alone therefore cannot supply a reliable full interval name.
levelTwoQualitiesBuild.contextBody: Key and later chord function can explain a spelling choice. In these tasks, spelling is already supplied: count precisely what is written. Do not first replace notes with more convenient enharmonic names. Use sound afterwards as a check.

levelTwoInversion.articleTitle: Interval inversion, direction and octave relationships
levelTwoInversion.invertTitle: Move an endpoint by an octave
levelTwoInversion.invertBody: To invert a simple interval, move its lower endpoint up an octave or its upper endpoint down an octave. The endpoints exchange order within the octave. C–E becomes E–C in the next register: a sixth, rather than a third simply played downwards.
levelTwoInversion.invertCaption: C–E, followed by its inversion E–C
levelTwoInversion.nineBody: Simple interval inversion numbers add to 9: second and seventh, third and sixth, fourth and fifth. Unison and octave form the edge case. Include both endpoints again. The octave displacement is part of the inversion.
levelTwoInversion.qualityBody: Perfect remains perfect; minor and major exchange. Augmented becomes diminished and diminished becomes augmented. A major third therefore inverts to a minor sixth. Adding the numbers is not enough: check quality as well.
levelTwoInversion.qualityCaption: Minor sixth as inversion of a major third
levelTwoInversion.descendingTitle: Count from the upper starting pitch
levelTwoInversion.descendingBody: When building downwards, preserve the named starting pitch. For a descending third from E, count E as 1, D as 2 and C as 3. Direction changes the letter sequence. This differs from the octave displacement used for inversion.
levelTwoInversion.downQualityBody: A descending major third from C reaches A-flat, four semitones lower. A is only three semitones lower, a minor third. First count descending letters, then sounding distance. Crossing below C also changes the register.
levelTwoInversion.downCheckBody: A descending perfect fifth from G reaches C. G, F, E, D, C are five counted letters; sounding distance is seven semitones downwards. It remains a perfect fifth rather than becoming a fourth because of its direction.
levelTwoInversion.compoundBody: A ninth is octave plus second; a tenth is octave plus third. Adding an octave raises the interval number by 7, not 8, because the shared endpoint counts once. Sounding distance increases by twelve semitones.
levelTwoInversion.compoundCaption: Major ninth: octave plus major second
levelTwoInversion.reduceBody: A major tenth reduces by one octave to a major third. Subtract 7 from the number while preserving quality. A minor ninth reduces to a minor second. This maps the interval class; the actual upper register remains visible in the score.
levelTwoInversion.reduceCaption: Major tenth maps to major third
levelTwoInversion.octavesBody: A perfect double octave has number 15. Removing one octave leaves a simple octave. Reduction stops within the simple interval range from unison through octave; a simple octave is therefore not reduced further to unison. Read the question carefully.

levelTwoMajor.patternTitle: Whole and half in a fixed order
levelTwoMajor.patternBody: A major scale follows 2–2–1–2–2–2–1 semitones. Its half steps lie between degrees 3–4 and 7–8. This pattern stays the same when the tonic changes. Read adjacent pitches rather than counting visible accidentals.
levelTwoMajor.patternCaption: C major with half steps E–F and B–C
levelTwoMajor.lettersBody: A seven-note major scale uses its seven letter names in order. The eighth pitch repeats the tonic one octave higher. Accidentals adjust sounding distances while retaining the letter sequence. G major therefore uses F-sharp rather than G-flat.
levelTwoMajor.lettersCaption: G major: one sharp on F
levelTwoMajor.transposeTitle: Apply the pattern from a new tonic
levelTwoMajor.transposeBody: Starting from F, natural notes would put a whole step between degrees 3 and 4. B-flat lowers degree four to create the required half step. German calls this lowered B-natural B; internationally it is B♭. The major pattern works in flat keys too.
levelTwoMajor.buildBody: The starting pitch stays fixed when writing a scale. Supply the next seven pitches through the octave. Choose each letter before its alteration. A correct sounding key with the wrong letter does not satisfy this spelling task.
levelTwoMajor.buildCaption: D major uses F-sharp and C-sharp
levelTwoMajor.threeBody: Writing tasks use major keys with zero through three sharps or flats: C, G, D, A and F, B-flat, E-flat. Octave is part of every answer. The next C after B starts the next scientific octave number; check this boundary carefully.
levelTwoMajor.threeCaption: A major: F-sharp, C-sharp and G-sharp
levelTwoMajor.checkBody: Check the letter sequence and then all seven sounding distances. A correctly written major scale needs both. Afterwards, hear the complete scale; its ending repeats the tonic in a higher register. An error review uses a different scale source.
levelTwoMajor.tonicBody: The $t(glossary:tonic_one) is the tonic of the key. In G major, G is degree one rather than C. The example’s starting pitch explicitly establishes that mapping. Degrees are positions within a scale rather than absolute piano-key numbers.
levelTwoMajor.tonicCaption: G is degree 1; B is degree 3
levelTwoMajor.degreesBody: Assign degrees 1 through 7 to the ascending scale notes. The octave endpoint is the tonic again. An accidental changes a degree’s sounding pitch rather than its position number. These tasks name a full pitch for you to locate in the scale shown.
levelTwoMajor.degreesCaption: B-flat is degree 4 in F major
levelTwoMajor.relationBody: C is the tonic of C major but degree four in G major. Its role depends on the scale. Answer degree questions after checking the starting pitch and major pattern. This prepares you to build diatonic triads later.
levelTwoMajor.relationCaption: C as degree four in G major

levelTwoMinor.naturalBody: Natural minor follows 2–1–2–2–1–2–2 semitones. Degree three is a minor third above the tonic. A natural minor uses natural notes from A through A; other tonics need alterations. The letter sequence remains ordered.
levelTwoMinor.thirdTitle: The minor third as a feature
levelTwoMinor.thirdBody: Major and natural minor differ in degree three: C major uses E and C minor E-flat. Natural minor also lowers degrees six and seven relative to same-tonic major. One isolated note does not automatically establish a real piece’s key; here you explicitly hear and write complete scales.
levelTwoMinor.thirdCaption: C minor with E-flat, A-flat and B-flat
levelTwoMinor.minorSignatureBody: Natural minor preserves the pitches of its key signature. E minor has F-sharp; G minor has B-flat and E-flat. The next key unit studies these signatures systematically. Here check written pitches against the natural-minor pattern.
levelTwoMinor.seventhBody: In this scale model, harmonic minor raises natural minor’s seventh degree by one semitone. In A minor, G becomes G-sharp, leaving a half step to A. The key signature remains that of A natural minor.
levelTwoMinor.augmentedSecondBody: F and G-sharp in A harmonic minor are three semitones apart. Their adjacent letters make an augmented second rather than a minor third. This scale still needs every letter in order. Sounding distance must not replace spelling.
levelTwoMinor.raiseTitle: A raised degree is relative to its existing pitch
levelTwoMinor.raiseBody: Raising does not always mean adding a sharp. Natural C minor has B-flat as degree seven; harmonic minor changes it to B-natural. Compare the natural starting form with the target pitch. The task evaluates the resulting exact spelling.
levelTwoMinor.melodicUpTitle: Raise degrees six and seven ascending
levelTwoMinor.melodicUpBody: Classical melodic minor ascending raises degrees six and seven of natural minor by one semitone each. In A minor these become F-sharp and G-sharp. The pattern is 2–1–2–2–2–2–1. The minor third above the tonic remains.
levelTwoMinor.melodicDownBody: In this classical teaching model, melodic minor descending returns to natural-minor degrees. Descending from A gives G, F, E, D, C, B and A. A recognition task must not offer this as a sounding alternative to descending natural minor.
levelTwoMinor.melodicDownCaption: A melodic minor descending: natural degrees
levelTwoMinor.conventionBody: Real melodies use raised or natural degrees according to musical context rather than always following direction. Jazz teaching may retain ascending melodic minor’s raised degrees when descending too. These tasks explicitly use the classical scale convention to make both directions unambiguous.

levelTwoKeys.articleTitle: Signatures, circle of fifths and related keys
levelTwoKeys.signatureTitle: A signature applies in every octave
levelTwoKeys.signatureBody: A $t(glossary:keySignature_one) applies to its letter names in every octave until changed. A local accidental can alter it within a measure. These tasks explicitly supply major or minor, because the same signature belongs to two relative keys.
levelTwoKeys.signatureCaption: G major: the signature raises every F
levelTwoKeys.sharpsBody: The first three sharps belong to F, C and G, producing G, D and A major from C major. Each added sharp retains earlier ones; any three letter positions will not do. The final sharp is one semitone below the major tonic.
levelTwoKeys.flatsBody: The first three flats belong to B, E and A: B-flat, E-flat and A-flat. Their major keys are F, B-flat and E-flat. German distinguishes H and B; internationally these are B and B♭. Check both actual signs and the naming language.
levelTwoKeys.flatsCaption: E-flat major with B-flat, E-flat and A-flat
levelTwoKeys.fifthsBody: On the $t(glossary:circleOfFifths), C and G are neighbours, as are G and D. An ascending fifth moves one signature step towards sharps. It can first remove a flat, as F major to C major does. This lesson’s tasks stay in major.
levelTwoKeys.backwardsBody: A descending fifth from C reaches F. This moves one circle step towards flats. From D major, the same step reaches G major and removes one sharp. The task states direction and mode; do not also change major to minor.
levelTwoKeys.nearbyBody: Neighbouring major keys differ by one signature step. E-flat–B-flat–F–C–G–D–A lists this stage’s seven keys. Sounding fifths and signature order check the same relationship in two ways. This is not alphabetical ordering.
levelTwoKeys.nearbyCaption: F–C connects the flat and sharp directions
levelTwoKeys.minorKeysBody: A minor has no signature accidentals, E minor one sharp and B minor two. D, G and C minor use one, two and three flats. The signature describes the natural-minor basis; harmonic or melodic minor’s raised degrees appear as additional accidentals in the music.
levelTwoKeys.minorKeysCaption: E minor: F-sharp in the signature; D-sharp as an additional raised degree
levelTwoKeys.relativeBody: $t(glossary:relativeKey_other) share a signature but have different tonics and modes. C major pairs with A minor and G major with E minor. The minor tonic lies a minor third below the major tonic. Sharing a signature therefore does not mean sharing a key.
levelTwoKeys.relativeCaption: C major and A minor: no signature accidentals
levelTwoKeys.parallelBody: German Paralleltonarten are English relative keys. Same-tonic major/minor pairs are German Varianttonarten and English parallel keys, such as C major and C minor. They share a tonic but have different signatures. This lesson always asks for the pair sharing a signature.
levelTwoKeys.parallelCaption: E-flat major and C minor share three flats

levelTwoQualities.stackBody: A $t(glossary:triad_one) in root position contains root, third and fifth. These roles refer to the chord root. C–E–G stacks the thirds C–E and E–G. Three arbitrary simultaneous notes are therefore not automatically a triad of this form.
levelTwoQualities.rolesBody: From root C, E is the third letter position and G the fifth. Accidentals determine the quality of these distances. The first tasks show root position so you can identify the roles confidently. Chord inversions follow in the next unit.
levelTwoQualities.rolesCaption: D is root; F third; A fifth
levelTwoQualities.fifthBody: Major and minor have a perfect fifth between root and fifth. Their third distinguishes major from minor. Diminished and augmented triads also alter the outer fifth. Include the written letter positions for every chord member.
levelTwoQualities.fifthCaption: F–C forms the outer perfect fifth
levelTwoQualities.majorBody: A root-position major triad has a major third below a minor third: four plus three semitones. C–E–G is the reference model. Writing preserves the root; supply the third and fifth with their exact names and registers.
levelTwoQualities.minorBody: A minor triad has a minor third below a major third: three plus four semitones. Its outer fifth remains perfect. C–E-flat–G differs from C–E–G only at the third. The letter E remains degree three even with a flat.
levelTwoQualities.writeChordBody: Enter the two missing chord members separately, then check the complete triad. Their input order is flexible; letter and octave still matter. A sounding equivalent with another spelling does not replace the required chord third or fifth.
levelTwoQualities.writeChordCaption: D major: its third requires F-sharp
levelTwoQualities.diminishedBody: A diminished triad stacks two minor thirds: three plus three semitones. Its outer diminished fifth spans six semitones. B–D–F is a natural-note model. In root position B is its root.
levelTwoQualities.augmentedBody: An augmented triad stacks two major thirds: four plus four semitones. Its outer fifth is augmented. C–E–G-sharp preserves the C, E and G letter roles. Its symmetric sound needs a supplied root reference in aural tasks; spelling can establish that role clearly.
levelTwoQualities.fourBody: Compare the two thirds: major 4+3, minor 3+4, diminished 3+3, augmented 4+4. This table describes close root position and does not replace correct spelling. This lesson writes diminished and augmented triads; later aural tasks compare all four.
levelTwoQualities.fourCaption: Diminished and augmented on the same root

levelTwoInversions.articleTitle: Chord roles, inversions and diatonic triads
levelTwoInversions.rootBassTitle: The lowest pitch is the bass
levelTwoInversions.rootBassBody: The $t(glossary:bassNote_one) is the lowest actual written or sounding chord pitch. The $t(glossary:root_one) determines chord identity. In E–G–C, E is bass and C is root. The chord remains a C-major triad.
levelTwoInversions.rootBassCaption: E in the bass; C as root
levelTwoInversions.reorderBody: Mentally reorder the letter roles into root position. Octave displacement does not change a member’s role. The complete written triad structure helps identify its root. The first or lowest note in a list is therefore not a reliable root rule.
levelTwoInversions.reorderCaption: G in the bass; still C major
levelTwoInversions.fixedRoleBody: C–E–G, E–G–C and G–C–E are three close positions of the same triad. Their ordering above the bass changes, not their major quality. Root, third and fifth remain attached to the same letter names. Check registers when comparing.
levelTwoInversions.fixedRoleCaption: Root position and first inversion of C major
levelTwoInversions.firstTitle: Third in the bass: first inversion
levelTwoInversions.firstBody: With the chord third in the bass, the triad is in first $t(glossary:inversion_one). German classical terminology calls this a Sextakkord. E–G–C has a third and sixth above E. C remains the chord root.
levelTwoInversions.secondTitle: Fifth in the bass: second inversion
levelTwoInversions.secondBody: With the chord fifth in the bass, the triad is in second inversion. German Quartsextakkord describes the fourth and sixth above its bass. G–C–E is C major’s second inversion. These tasks ask for quality and inversion together.
levelTwoInversions.recognizeBody: Identify the written triad and its root first. Then compare the lowest pitch with root, third and fifth. This determines root position, first inversion or second inversion. Augmented and diminished triads follow the same role rule.
levelTwoInversions.recognizeCaption: C minor with third E-flat in the bass
levelTwoInversions.diatonicBody: Diatonic triads stack thirds within the actual scale. On degree n, take n, n+2 and n+4, continuing in the next octave above seven. In C major, D, F and A form a minor triad on degree two.
levelTwoInversions.diatonicCaption: Degree 2 in C major: D minor
levelTwoInversions.majorDegreesBody: Major follows major, minor, minor, major, major, minor, diminished. The sequence follows from scale notes rather than an arbitrary quality choice. The writing task names key and degree and supplies the chord root; add only the matching diatonic notes.
levelTwoInversions.minorDegreesBody: Natural minor follows minor, diminished, major, minor, minor, major, major. Harmonic minor’s raised seventh would produce different triads. These tasks therefore explicitly use natural minor. Check key, degree and the resulting stacked pitches.
levelTwoInversions.minorDegreesCaption: Degree 5 in A natural minor: E minor

levelTwoRhythmDetail.longShortBody: A dotted quarter followed by an eighth divides two quarter-note values in a 3:1 ratio. Hear the complete phrase before matching onsets to the three score options. The source preserves actual rests and durations; identical pitches isolate rhythm here.
levelTwoRhythmDetail.shortLongBody: Eighth plus dotted quarter has the same total duration as the reverse order. Its second onset occurs at a different position. Compare note starts rather than only the final ending. Both patterns can appear among the score options.
levelTwoRhythmDetail.shortLongCaption: Short–long: the second onset arrives earlier
levelTwoRhythmDetail.smallValuesBody: Dotted eighth plus sixteenth divides one quarter-note value unequally. A rest shifts later onsets without making a sound itself. Count equal small subdivisions while listening. The matching score must preserve onsets and rest durations.
levelTwoRhythmDetail.smallValuesCaption: Dotted eighth, sixteenth, and a later rest
levelTwoRhythmDetail.twoPartsBody: The higher note marks each beat’s start in these teaching models. Duple subdivision has two equal notes per beat: the higher start and one lower note. Count the start as the first part and stop before the next higher note.
levelTwoRhythmDetail.threePartsBody: Triple subdivision groups the higher start with two lower subdivisions. The next higher note starts a new group. This task explicitly contrasts duple and triple beats; it does not ask for meter identification from ambiguous sound.
levelTwoRhythmDetail.tempoReferenceBody: The task uses beats as its tempo reference: quarters in 2/4 and dotted quarters in 6/8. This makes duple and triple groups comparable at the same beat rate. Introduction examples instead use the stated quarter-note reference at tempo 90.
levelTwoRhythmDetail.outlineBody: The visible outline shows only the first three quarter-note beats of a 4/4 measure. Audio plays the complete measure. Every answer score spans one quarter-note value and supplies only missing beat four. The empty space is not a written rest.
levelTwoRhythmDetail.completeBody: Focus on the final beat and retain whether it contains a long note, two equal short notes or an unequal pair. You can replay the whole source. The previous three quarters provide a time reference; they are not the queried cell.
levelTwoRhythmDetail.completeCaption: Beat four contains dotted eighth plus sixteenth
levelTwoRhythmDetail.silenceBody: A cell can end in silence. Identifying its first onset alone is insufficient; also check how long it sounds. Evaluation compares onsets and durations from the same complete source. The question concerns rhythm rather than instrument colour.
levelTwoRhythmDetail.silenceCaption: Beat four ends with an eighth rest

levelTwoMelody.secondsBody: A minor second spans one semitone; a major second spans two. Hear both notes in sequence and compare their distance. Absolute pitch naming is unnecessary. These tasks offer only intervals with distinct sounding distances.
levelTwoMelody.secondsCaption: Minor second followed by major second
levelTwoMelody.thirdsSixthsBody: Minor and major thirds span three and four semitones; minor and major sixths span eight and nine. Compare wider distances with their interval family and octave frame. The task’s source plays the lower note first.
levelTwoMelody.thirdsSixthsCaption: Major third/minor sixth and minor third/major sixth
levelTwoMelody.frameBody: Perfect fourth, fifth and octave span five, seven and twelve semitones. Minor seventh lies two semitones below the octave; major seventh lies one below. Sounding equivalents such as augmented fourth and diminished fifth are not offered against each other here.
levelTwoMelody.frameCaption: Fourth, fifth, minor/major seventh and octave
levelTwoMelody.majorSoundBody: The source ascends from tonic to octave. Major places degree three a major third above the starting pitch. Its remaining whole- and half-step sequence also matters. Judge the complete sequence rather than a supposed colour of a specific key.
levelTwoMelody.majorSoundCaption: Major scale as one continuous listening sequence
levelTwoMelody.minorSoundBody: From the same tonic, natural minor has a minor third and lower sixth and seventh degrees than major. First and last notes provide the frame. This task uses only ascending major and natural minor so the answers remain aurally distinct.
levelTwoMelody.minorSoundCaption: Natural minor from the same tonic C
levelTwoMelody.transposeEarBody: The distance pattern identifies the model at other tonics too. A G-major sequence remains major and an E-minor sequence remains natural minor. Varying tonics trains relationships rather than one memorized pitch sequence. Inability to listen is counted separately as a skip.
levelTwoMelody.rememberBody: The melodic-memory task plays two sources of four equal-duration notes separated by a short pause. Count 1 through 4 and retain their contour. Exactly one pitch changes in source B; rhythm and the other positions remain the same.
levelTwoMelody.rememberCaption: Four fixed pitch positions in the first model
levelTwoMelody.locateBody: The question asks for the changed note’s position rather than its absolute name. Compare A and B note by note. If only pitch three differs, choose note 3. Replay both sources if needed; the separating pause is not part of the melody.
levelTwoMelody.locateCaption: G replaces F at position 3 in the second model
levelTwoMelody.reviewMemoryBody: An error review changes both sounding source and target answer rather than only shuffling buttons. In melodic memory, a different one of the four positions can be queried. Retain the new source instead of blindly repeating an earlier answer.

levelTwoTriads.rootReferenceBody: Each chord question first plays the root alone as a reference, then the triad. This establishes chord identity without absolute pitch. Hear the combined shape of its three notes afterwards. The score stays hidden before evaluation.
levelTwoTriads.hearThirdTitle: The third makes the first difference
levelTwoTriads.hearThirdBody: With the same root, major and minor share a perfect fifth. Their middle root-position pitch forms a major or minor third above the root. Compare the two models. Labels such as happy or sad are not reliable grading rules for all music.
levelTwoTriads.hearThirdCaption: Major and minor with the same outer fifth
levelTwoTriads.wholeChordBody: The chord’s three notes sound together. You can mentally organize them into roles from the root, but the source is not a scale run. First tasks use root-position major and minor. Changing the root does not change the quality rule.
levelTwoTriads.diminishedEarBody: A diminished triad stacks two minor thirds and has a diminished fifth above its root. Compare it with minor’s perfect outer fifth. This lesson uses root position throughout. The preceding reference pitch is part of the task.
levelTwoTriads.augmentedEarBody: An augmented triad stacks two major thirds. Its symmetric sound permits several enharmonic root interpretations without a reference. The task therefore supplies and plays the root. Choose quality relative to it rather than guessing an absolute root from the chord alone.
levelTwoTriads.compareFourBody: Retain four quality models with a root reference: major, minor, diminished and augmented. Answer options do not alter the source. After grading, compare the actual notation with the chord heard. Sounding equivalents are not offered as distinct enharmonic aural answers.
levelTwoTriads.bassEarTitle: Compare the bass with the reference
levelTwoTriads.bassEarBody: The lowest chord pitch’s role determines inversion. The root reference plays separately beforehand. Third in the bass indicates first inversion; fifth in the bass indicates second. These tasks use close-position major and minor triads.
levelTwoTriads.bassEarCaption: C root reference; third E in the bass
levelTwoTriads.closePositionBody: Here the three pitches occupy close position without large gaps. This supports targeted comparison of root position and both inversions. Real music may use wider spacing and doublings; these tasks do not yet ask for a general analysis of performing forces.
levelTwoTriads.closePositionCaption: C root reference; fifth G in the bass
levelTwoTriads.qualityPositionBody: The final lesson combines two decisions: major or minor, and root position or one of two inversions. Retain the root reference and identify the bass role. Review changes the actual reference or chord sound; merely renaming it is insufficient.

levelTwoPeriodContexts.medievalBody: The European overview places a teaching dossier dated 1250 in the Middle Ages. Monophonic liturgical singing is one possible feature, rather than the period’s only music. Secular traditions and polyphonic practices also existed. The original piano model is neither a medieval recording nor a historical work.
levelTwoPeriodContexts.medievalCaption: Original monophonic teaching model; no historical recording
levelTwoPeriodContexts.renaissanceBody: An explicitly supplied composition year of 1550 fits the Renaissance in our European overview. Imitative vocal polyphony is a common feature: voices take up related musical ideas. Genre, occasion and region still matter. This monophonic piano pattern is only an original sequence, not an authentic polyphonic source.
levelTwoPeriodContexts.renaissanceCaption: Original illustrative sequence; not a Renaissance work
levelTwoPeriodContexts.firstContextBody: Tasks explicitly provide a composition year and a feature in a fictional teaching dossier. Match both to the broad overview. One melody, instrument or modern recording alone cannot securely date composition. Period transitions overlap across regions and genres.
levelTwoPeriodContexts.firstContextCaption: A generic interval model does not date a work
levelTwoPeriodContexts.baroqueBody: A teaching dossier dated 1720 fits the Baroque here. $t(glossary:continuo) combines a bass foundation with chordal realization; instruments and execution can vary. Church, court, opera and instrumental genres served different functions. A bass motif alone does not establish Baroque provenance.
levelTwoPeriodContexts.baroqueCaption: Original bass foundation as a teaching model
levelTwoPeriodContexts.classicalBody: This overview places composition year 1780 in the Classical period. Regular phrases and periodic construction are common teaching features rather than universal or exclusive traits. Courtly and public concert contexts overlap. The fictional dossier explicitly supplies its date.
levelTwoPeriodContexts.baroqueClassicalBody: Baroque and Classical describe broad historical contexts rather than labels guaranteed by one sonic detail. Compare composition year, function and stated features. A modern arrangement can combine older and newer traits. Distinguish composition from performance dates.
levelTwoPeriodContexts.baroqueClassicalCaption: A closing gesture can occur in many contexts
levelTwoPeriodContexts.romanticBody: Composition year 1850 fits this overview’s Romantic period. Expanded chromaticism, individual expression and changing public musical cultures are possible contexts. They do not replace source checking. Romantic music is not uniformly programmatic, large-scale or alike in sound.
levelTwoPeriodContexts.since1900Body: Music since 1900 is not a single style. Tonal, expanded and differently organized pitch systems coexist with new media and electronic sound production. The teaching dossier dated 1950 explicitly mentions electronics. The piano model is not an electronic or historical original recording.
levelTwoPeriodContexts.since1900Caption: Original pitch sequence; no style dating from sound
levelTwoPeriodContexts.limitsBody: These six periods mainly organize European art-music history, not a universal chronology of all musical traditions. Task years intentionally avoid transition boundaries. Real works and sources need more precise regional, social and genre-specific interpretation.

levelTwoJazzPopSources.articleTitle: Jazz, popular music and source criticism
levelTwoJazzPopSources.communitiesBody: Early jazz developments are closely tied to African American musical practice and United States social contexts. Blues, ragtime, dance, brass-band and other musical cultures interact. One person, record or city story cannot replace this context. Tasks explicitly use fictional social teaching dossiers.
levelTwoJazzPopSources.communitiesCaption: Original pitch sequence, not a historical jazz recording
levelTwoJazzPopSources.migrationBody: African American migration from the South to northern cities also changed musical networks, venues and media contacts. A report of relocation documents that social context. It does not establish that the music did not previously exist. Region, people and perspective remain source questions.
levelTwoJazzPopSources.migrationCaption: Original model accompanying the source text
levelTwoJazzPopSources.recordBusinessTitle: Recording history is not origin history
levelTwoJazzPopSources.recordBusinessBody: The first commercially issued or surviving recording does not establish a musical tradition’s first origin. Companies, access conditions and racist exclusions affected what was documented and distributed. Distinguish musical practice from media history. A studio file initially documents recording business.
levelTwoJazzPopSources.recordBusinessCaption: Original chord model; not an archival recording
levelTwoJazzPopSources.popularBody: Popular music includes different genres, audiences and forms of distribution. A recording belongs to a particular production and social setting. Ask who made, published or distributed it. A media label such as radio or stream does not automatically describe its complete musical origins.
levelTwoJazzPopSources.popularCaption: Original short sequence; not borrowed from a popular song
levelTwoJazzPopSources.productionBody: Microphones, editing, mixing and other production choices shape a recording. Its documented sound need not match an unrecorded performance. The medium preserves released or surviving sound; production process and original performing forces require additional sources.
levelTwoJazzPopSources.productionCaption: Original piano model without a claimed studio history
levelTwoJazzPopSources.distributionBody: $t(glossary:broadcast_other) and $t(glossary:stream_other) distribute music through different technical and commercial systems. A broadcast or release date dates distribution rather than automatically dating composition. Task sources therefore distinguish recordings, announcements, reports and media channels.
levelTwoJazzPopSources.distributionCaption: Original rhythm model accompanying the media topic
levelTwoJazzPopSources.datesBody: A work can predate its recording by many years. Different composition and recording dates are therefore not contradictory. First identify each date’s claim. Different dates assigned to the same performance are instead an unresolved conflict requiring more evidence.
levelTwoJazzPopSources.datesCaption: A model’s sound alone supplies no composition date
levelTwoJazzPopSources.intentBody: A program can advertise performing forces; a performance report can describe who actually appeared. These are different claims even for the same event. A recording can help check sound, but does not replace every piece of information about names and roles.
levelTwoJazzPopSources.intentCaption: Simultaneous and single sound as an original observation model
levelTwoJazzPopSources.uncertaintyBody: Two agreeing sources may copy one another. Check their independence before treating them as double corroboration. State open questions and distinguish observation from inference. These tasks grade justified limits on claims rather than the most persuasive guess.
levelTwoJazzPopSources.uncertaintyCaption: Original four-note model without a provenance claim

firstLesson.title: Discover notes and intervals
firstLesson.notesTitle: Note names in the treble clef
firstLesson.notesBody: A $t(glossary:staff_one) has five lines. Spaces and ledger lines continue the sequence C, D, E, F, G, A, B. In the $t(glossary:trebleClef_one), G4 is on the second line from the bottom. A $t(glossary:sharp_one) raises a note by one $t(glossary:semitone_one); a $t(glossary:flat_one) lowers it by one $t(glossary:semitone_one).
firstLesson.intervalsBody: An $t(glossary:interval_one) is the distance between two notes. Count the letter names, including both ends: C–E spans three, so it is a third. Minor and major thirds differ in sound distance: three or four $t(glossary:semitone_other). C–E♭ is minor; C–E is major.
firstLesson.hearingBody: A $t(glossary:semitone_one) is the smallest distance between adjacent piano keys, including the black keys. C–F spans four letter names and five $t(glossary:semitone_other): a perfect fourth. C–G spans five letter names and seven $t(glossary:semitone_other): a perfect fifth. Compare these sounds with the thirds. Every listening question plays the lower note first.

notationStart.staffBody: A $t(glossary:staff_one) has five lines and four spaces. Count the lines from bottom to top. A $t(glossary:note_one) can sit on a line or in a space. Its position helps you read the $t(glossary:pitch_one). In this example, the note is on the second line from the bottom. The $t(glossary:clef_one) at the beginning tells you which pitch that line represents.
notationStart.anchorBody: The $t(glossary:trebleClef_one) places G4 on the second line from the bottom. It is also called the G clef. The $t(glossary:naturalNote_other) are C, D, E, F, G, A, B; then the letter sequence repeats. A $t(glossary:naturalNote_one) is a note without a raised or lowered pitch. These questions do not yet use $t(glossary:accidental_other).
notationStart.neighborsTitle: Find the notes next to G
notationStart.neighborsBody: Move from a line to the next space or from a space to the next line: you reach the next $t(glossary:naturalNote_one). Below G4 is F4 in the first space; above it are A4 in the second space and B4 on the third line. Read this example as F, G, A, B. This lesson only asks for these four note names. The international B corresponds to the German H.
notationStart.linesBody: In the $t(glossary:trebleClef_one), the five line notes from bottom to top are E, G, B, D, F. Another $t(glossary:naturalNote_one) sits in the space between each pair of lines. Use G on the second line as your reference: one position below it is F, and one more is E. Include the spaces when counting. The questions ask for the note name, not yet its exact $t(glossary:octave_one).
notationStart.spacesBody: The four spaces in the $t(glossary:trebleClef_one) are F, A, C, E from bottom to top. Lines and spaces alternate. Together, from the lowest to the highest line, they give E, F, G, A, B, C, D, E, F. Look at the centre of the notehead: it shows the position, not the end of the stem.
notationStart.namesBody: After B comes C again. The $t(glossary:naturalNote_other) form the repeating sequence C, D, E, F, G, A, B. Their positions rise as you move up the $t(glossary:staff_one), and fall as you move down. This example includes E and F twice, each in a different register. When asked for the note name, the answer remains E or F in both registers. You will learn the exact $t(glossary:octave_one) in a later unit.
notationStart.readingBody: Check the $t(glossary:clef_one) first. Find the line or space of the notehead. Count $t(glossary:naturalNote_other) from the known G on the second line to the required position. Listen to the example when you choose to. Start by reading G, A, B, C, D, C, B, A; the audio plays that same sequence. Hints explain how to count, and mistakes are followed by new notes in the review.
notationStart.anchorCaption: G4 on the second line from the bottom
notationStart.namesCaption: All nine positions: E4 to F5
notationStart.staffArticle: A $t(glossary:note_one) combines several kinds of information. The position of its notehead on the $t(glossary:staff_one), together with the $t(glossary:clef_one), describes its $t(glossary:pitch_one). Its shape indicates its value; you will study note values in the rhythm area. Keep those questions separate at first: here you read pitch. Five lines and four spaces give nine positions within the stave. Count from the lowest line. Later, positions outside the stave need $t(glossary:ledgerLine_other).
notationStart.anchorArticle: The $t(glossary:trebleClef_one) is a G clef: it identifies the second line from the bottom as G4, or g¹ in German notation. Alternating lines and spaces lead from that reference through the sequence of $t(glossary:naturalNote_other). These letter steps are not equal distances in sound; the next notation unit covers $t(glossary:semitone_other) and $t(glossary:wholeTone_other). The $t(glossary:naturalNote_other) C, D, E, F, G, A, B are unaltered notes. The international B corresponds to German H; German B means the lowered H. These questions do not use alterations.
notationStart.namesArticle: In the $t(glossary:trebleClef_one), E, G, B, D, F sit on the five lines, and F, A, C, E occupy the four spaces. Together they read E, F, G, A, B, C, D, E, F. The letter sequence starts again at C after B while the pitch continues to rise. A note name can therefore appear in several $t(glossary:octave_other). International notation uses E4 and E5, for example; German notation uses e¹ and e². This exercise set only asks for the note name E. A later unit practises the complete octave register.
notationStart.readingArticle: For each new note, check the $t(glossary:clef_one), then the position of the notehead, then the letter sequence. Work step by step from the known G or use line and space notes you already know reliably. Check your reading with the audio example; you do not need to guess the note name from sound alone. Short, regular sets build confidence, and a longer mixed set consolidates the same basics. Each run generates new questions. A mistake leads to a different written note in the review so that you apply the reading method again.

keyboardStart.groupsBody: On a $t(glossary:keyboard_one), $t(glossary:twoBlackKeys_other) alternate with $t(glossary:threeBlackKeys_other). The white key immediately left of a group of two is C; to the left of a group of three is F. Dots mark C and F in the picture. Sound examples only start when you choose to play them.
keyboardStart.whiteBody: The white $t(glossary:pianoKey_other) carry the $t(glossary:naturalNote_other) C, D, E, F, G, A, B. The sequence then starts again at C. This example shows eight white keys up to the next C. The key questions use a smaller fixed range from C to B: each natural note name occurs exactly once. The international B is called H in German.
keyboardStart.findTitle: Find a key from its name
keyboardStart.findBody: Find C to the left of the group of two black keys, or F to the left of the group of three. Follow the white keys to the requested name. The questions ask for the note name; the exact $t(glossary:octave_one) comes in the next unit. Select the matching key, then choose Check. The higher and lower views help you read sideways; they keep this fixed range. On a computer keyboard, you can also reach the keys with Tab.
keyboardStart.stepsBody: A $t(glossary:semitone_one) reaches the immediately adjacent $t(glossary:pianoKey_one), whether it is white or black. C to C♯ is one step, and C♯ to D is another. A $t(glossary:wholeTone_one) consists of two $t(glossary:semitone_other): exactly one key lies between C and D. Count the moves between keys; the starting and ending keys are not extra steps.
keyboardStart.neighborsTitle: E–F and B–C are directly adjacent
keyboardStart.neighborsBody: There is no black key between E and F. There is also no key between B and the next C. Each distance is one $t(glossary:semitone_one). Between C and D, however, there is a black key; that distance is a $t(glossary:wholeTone_one). Select the two examples separately and compare their notation, marked keys and sound.
keyboardStart.signsBody: A $t(glossary:sharp_one) ♯ raises a $t(glossary:naturalNote_one) by one $t(glossary:semitone_one); move one key to the right. A $t(glossary:flat_one) ♭ lowers it by one $t(glossary:semitone_one); move one key to the left. A $t(glossary:natural_one) ♮ cancels a currently applied alteration. The third example shows G♯ followed by G with a natural sign in the same $t(glossary:measure_one). These questions only use single accidentals. Double accidentals and the exact rules for how long an accidental applies (to the end of the $t(glossary:measure_one)) come later.
keyboardStart.namesBody: International names use the letter followed by a sign: C♯, D♭ and E♭. In German these are Cis, Des and Es. International B is called H in German; B♭ is called B. The example B–B♭ moves one key to the left. The data and evaluation use the same pitches even when the language shows different names.
keyboardStart.sameBody: C♯ and D♭ name the same key on an equal-tempered piano. Their written notes are different. An accidental does not always mean a black key: E♯ sounds on the F key, and F♭ on the E key. A key question checks the physical key. A note-name question checks the displayed spelling: a written E♯ must be named E♯. Always find the requested natural note before following its alteration.
keyboardStart.groupsCaption: C left of the group of two; F left of the group of three
keyboardStart.findCaption: Find D and A in this range
keyboardStart.sharpCaption: G–G♯: one key to the right
