keyboardStart.flatCaption: A–A♭: one key to the left
keyboardStart.sameCaption: C♯ and D♭: the same key
keyboardStart.whiteSharpCaption: E♯ and F: the same white key
keyboardStart.whiteFlatCaption: F♭ and E: the same white key
keyboardStart.layoutArticle: The repeating arrangement of black keys helps you read the $t(glossary:keyboard_one). C is immediately to the left of a group of two, and F to the left of a group of three. From there, name the white keys C, D, E, F, G, A, B. The sequence repeats after B. In the first questions, each natural note name appears only once within the fixed range, so you do not yet have to distinguish octave registers. The picture also shows the next C to make that repetition visible. The notation connects the names to their sound; $t(glossary:ledgerLine_other) and exact registers will be covered in the following unit.
keyboardStart.stepsArticle: On an equal-tempered piano, adjacent keys are one $t(glossary:semitone_one) apart. Count moves, not the number of keys touched. C to C♯ and C♯ to D each take one step; C to D takes two and forms a $t(glossary:wholeTone_one). White and black keys count equally. E–F and B–the next C are directly adjacent, so they are $t(glossary:semitone_other). These exceptions show why neighbouring white keys are not always a $t(glossary:wholeTone_one) apart.
keyboardStart.signsArticle: A single $t(glossary:sharp_one) raises the written natural note by a $t(glossary:semitone_one); a single $t(glossary:flat_one) lowers it by a $t(glossary:semitone_one). The notehead stays at its natural-note position; the sign changes the pitch. A $t(glossary:natural_one) cancels a current alteration and returns to the unaltered natural note. In the G♯–G example, the natural sign appears in the same $t(glossary:measure_one). These questions contain no $t(glossary:keySignature_other) or double accidentals; a later block covers the complete rules for how accidentals apply.
keyboardStart.namesArticle: International names keep the note letter and add a sign, as in C♯, D♭ and E♭. German uses names such as Cis, Des and Es. One especially important difference is B/H: international B is German H, and international B♭ is German B. The move from B to B♭ lowers the pitch by a $t(glossary:semitone_one). Names and explanations are generated from the same language-independent pitch. Changing language changes neither sound nor key number.
keyboardStart.sameArticle: On an equal-tempered piano, differently spelled pitches can use the same key. C♯ and D♭ are one example; E♯/F and F♭/E show that accidentals can also lead to white keys. For a key question, the sounding pitch matters. A note-name question evaluates the letter and alteration together: E♯ and F remain different correct answers for their respective written notes. This distinction prepares the later topic of $t(glossary:enharmonic); further spellings and exact registers follow the basics.

registerStart.matchLesson: Play the written note on the $t(glossary:keyboard_one)
registerStart.repetitionTitle: The same letter in a different register
registerStart.repetitionBody: The letter sequence C, D, E, F, G, A, B repeats. E can lie lower or higher without changing its letter. An E and the next higher E are one $t(glossary:octave_one) apart. Their noteheads occupy different positions, and the dots mark different keys. Questions in this unit require the complete $t(glossary:noteName_one), including its $t(glossary:octaveRegister_one).
registerStart.boundaryTitle: A new register starts at C
registerStart.boundaryBody: An $t(glossary:octaveRegister_one) runs from C to B. The next C starts the next register. The neighbours shown are B4 and C5; German names are h¹ and c². The octave number changes here. The sound rises by one $t(glossary:semitone_one), even though the register number changes.
registerStart.namesBody: C4 and C5 name different notes and keys. F4 and F5 also have different complete names. German names use c¹/c² and f¹/f² respectively. Choose the name and register together; the same letter in a different register is a wrong answer. The first lesson stays within E4–F5, on the five lines and their spaces.
registerStart.extendTitle: Continue the stave beyond its edges
registerStart.extendBody: Lines and spaces continue beyond the five lines. D lies immediately below the bottom line, and G immediately above the top line; neither needs a $t(glossary:ledgerLine_one). The next line position receives a short line through the notehead. Count each neighbouring position from the known E4 or F5.
registerStart.lowerBody: In the $t(glossary:trebleClef_one), C4 lies on the first lower $t(glossary:ledgerLine_one). B3 occupies the next space, and A3 the second line. German names are c¹, h and a; a and h have no superscript in that notation. The stepwise example descends through D4, C4, B3 and A3. Include spaces as you count.
registerStart.upperBody: Above F5 come G5 in the outer space, A5 on the first $t(glossary:ledgerLine_one), B5 in the next space and C6 on the second line. German names are g², a², h² and c³. Compare the short example with the complete path upward. Questions use A3–C6 and need no more than two lines per note.
registerStart.matchTitle: Connect the written note to its sounding key
registerStart.matchBody: Read the complete $t(glossary:noteName_one) in the $t(glossary:trebleClef_one), including its $t(glossary:ledgerLine_other). Then find the key in the same register. C4 and C5 are different keys. The fixed range is A3–C6; reach keys to the side with Higher, Lower or Move. Question text does not name the target. All questions use $t(glossary:naturalNote_other).
registerStart.strategyTitle: Two steps to one complete answer
registerStart.strategyBody: First check the clef, notehead position and complete name. Then find the matching register on the piano keyboard and select the key. The same letter in a neighbouring register is a different key. Hint use is recorded separately; mistakes receive a different pitch in the review. Examples stay silent until you start the sound example.
registerStart.eCaption: E4 and E5: the same letter in neighbouring registers
registerStart.boundaryCaption: B4–C5: the register changes at C
registerStart.cCaption: C4 and C5: two different keys
registerStart.fCaption: F4 and F5: the complete name matters
registerStart.extendCaption: D4 and G5: outside the five lines with no ledger line
registerStart.lowerLinesCaption: C4 on one lower ledger line, A3 on two
registerStart.upperLinesCaption: A5 on one upper ledger line, C6 on two
registerStart.matchCCaption: C4 and C5 in the complete practice range
registerStart.matchEdgesCaption: A3 and C6: the edges of the practice range
registerStart.strategyCaption: Match G4, G5 and C5 confidently
registerStart.octavesArticle: A letter alone does not specify a unique pitch. The sequence C, D, E, F, G, A, B repeats in different $t(glossary:octaveRegister_other). A register starts at C and ends at B. B4 and C5 therefore change their register number even though their keys are neighbours. A note and its next higher counterpart with the same name are one $t(glossary:octave_one) apart. On an equal-tempered piano this is twelve $t(glossary:semitone_other). Here the register is read from notation; naming intervals is not a prerequisite.
registerStart.namesArticle: International display uses a letter and scientific octave number: A3, B3, C4, C5 and C6 are the relevant examples. German display uses Helmholtz names: a and h in the small register, c¹ to h¹ in the one-line register, c² to h² in the two-line register and c³ in the next. Data and answers store complete language-neutral pitches. The first lesson reads E4–F5 without extra lines. A full comparison of naming systems comes in Level 2; here you only need your selected language.
registerStart.lowerArticle: The $t(glossary:trebleClef_one) places G4 on the second line from the bottom. The bottom line carries E4. Below it come D4 in the outer space, C4 on one lower $t(glossary:ledgerLine_one), B3 in the next space and A3 on two lines. Each head remains in a line or space position. Short extra lines have the same spacing as the five main lines. The question checks name and register together.
registerStart.upperArticle: The top line in the $t(glossary:trebleClef_one) carries F5. Above it come G5 without an extra line, A5 on one upper $t(glossary:ledgerLine_one), B5 in the next space and C6 on two lines. Count extra lines outward from the stave edge. Space notes retain the extra lines already reached. The A3–C6 question range limits notation to two lines; more distant pitches are not yet assessed.
registerStart.matchArticle: A key answer must match the sounding pitch, including its $t(glossary:octaveRegister_one). C4 and C5 are different answers. Read the written pitch first, then find C in that register and follow the white keys to the name. The range stays A3–C6; sideways movement does not extend it. Question text does not name the target. Mistakes receive a different sounding pitch in the review; results and hints remain separate. The preceding keyboard unit introduces simple accidentals. Writing notes on a stave follows in Level 2.

pulseStart.groupsLesson: Count groups of two, three and four
pulseStart.pulseTitle: Steady beats as a timing reference
pulseStart.pulseBody: The $t(glossary:pulse) is the steady underlying beat. Like walking steps, its beats are evenly spaced here. A $t(glossary:metronome_one) makes them audible as clicks. Listen and count 1–2–3–4, then return to 1. The highlighted 1 starts a new group; its time interval is just as long as the others. Numbers show counting positions, not pitches. The BPM number gives the beats per minute; hear their spacing in the example.
pulseStart.rhythmTitle: Distinguish the underlying beat from the sound pattern
pulseStart.rhythmBody: $t(glossary:rhythm_one) is the sequence of sounds and rests in time. Individual sounds can be short or long while the $t(glossary:pulse) stays steady. In this unit, every click receives exactly one tap: no subdivisions or rests yet. The example shows only this steady reference. Note values and rhythm patterns follow in the next units; you do not need to read notation yet.
pulseStart.countInTitle: Listen first, then start on the next 1
pulseStart.countInBody: The $t(glossary:countIn) is one whole group of clicks before your entrance. It gives you the speed and starting point. The sound example plays two groups; imagine joining on the second 1. In a question, “Count in and record” starts the same lead-in. Begin tapping on the next accented 1, then tap every click once. The tap pad is locked during the count-in. Checking is available only after the whole recording.
pulseStart.tempoBody: $t(glossary:tempo) tells you how fast the underlying beats move. Here, $t(glossary:beatsPerMinute) measures the number of clicks in one minute. At 60 BPM, clicks are one second apart; at 120 BPM, half a second. Higher tempo means shorter intervals, lower tempo longer ones. Compare the two examples with the same four-beat group. Speed stays constant within a single question.
pulseStart.bpmTitle: The number refers to the underlying beat
pulseStart.bpmBody: BPM stands for “beats per minute”. Here it counts the evenly spaced clicks, not written notes. At 90 BPM, one interval lasts two thirds of a second: 60 seconds divided by 90. A group of three still has 90 beats per minute. Group size determines when counting returns to 1; it does not change the $t(glossary:tempo).
pulseStart.compareTitle: More beats per minute, shorter intervals
pulseStart.compareBody: Listen to the same group of three at 72 and 108 BPM. The second example is faster: the click intervals are shorter. The sequence 1–2–3 stays the same, and the accented 1 still starts the group. When a new question gives a different $t(glossary:tempo), listen to its whole $t(glossary:countIn). Avoid carrying over the previous question’s interval by accident.
pulseStart.groupsTitle: Return to 1 after the last position
pulseStart.groupsBody: A $t(glossary:beatGroup_one) combines evenly spaced beats: 1–2, 1–2–3 or 1–2–3–4. After the last beat, the next group starts at 1. Listen to the three examples at the same 84 BPM. The first position is accented, but no longer; all click intervals stay equal. This prepares you to count simple bars. Time signatures such as 3/4 and their note values are explained and assessed later.
pulseStart.strategyBody: Read the group size and BPM, listen to the whole count-in and tap every click from the next 1. Holding the button produces only one tap. After recording, check it or record again without a score. Missing or extra taps count as errors; hints count as assistance. A mistake receives a different group size in the separately scored review. “Cannot listen right now” skips tapping questions; term questions remain. Skipping or using assistance does not demonstrate an independently completed rhythm question.
pulseStart.steadyFasterCaption: The same group of four at 96 BPM
pulseStart.referenceCaption: Steady reference: one tap on every click
pulseStart.countInCaption: Two groups of three: enter on the second 1
pulseStart.hundredTwentyCaption: 120 BPM: half a second between clicks
pulseStart.ninetyCaption: 90 BPM: three counting positions per group
pulseStart.strategyCaption: Group of four at 96 BPM: one tap per click
pulseStart.pulseArticle: Steady underlying beats provide a timing reference. A $t(glossary:metronome_one) produces regular clicks. These exercises play one whole count-in cycle before recording a group of the same length. Intervals remain constant within a question; the first counting position is accented. The numbers help you match each counting position to one click. Counting and listening are enough for these exercises.
pulseStart.rhythmArticle: $t(glossary:pulse) and $t(glossary:rhythm_one) have different roles: the underlying beat remains a regular reference, while the sequence of sounds and rests above it can change. Here all required taps fall exactly on the clicks. The examples do not demonstrate uneven sound patterns. Reading longer, shorter or resting events belongs to the following units on note values and simple bars. Assessment checks the tap onset, not how long the pad stays pressed.
pulseStart.tempoArticle: $t(glossary:tempo) is the speed of the underlying beat. BPM counts these beats per minute; one interval lasts 60/BPM seconds. At 60 BPM that is one second; at 90 BPM two thirds; at 120 BPM half a second. A higher number produces shorter intervals. Two, three or four counting positions per group do not change the interval at the same BPM. The reference to a written beat value is introduced with time signatures later.
pulseStart.countInArticle: During the $t(glossary:countIn), listen to one whole group first. Recording starts on the next accented 1. Listen for the steady interval and count each position once. Use the sound as your timing reference when tapping; the visible count helps you follow the phases, but is not a precise timing cursor for a tap. A completed take can be checked even if it has no taps. Cancelling creates no answer; you can begin again with a new whole count-in group.
pulseStart.groupsArticle: Beat groups repeat 1–2, 1–2–3 or 1–2–3–4 with equal beat durations. The accented 1 marks the group’s start in these examples. Numbers alone do not explain a full time signature; denominators, note values and compound metres come later. The three lessons combine term questions with four, six or eight tapping questions. Mistakes receive new group sizes; hints and skipping are stored separately. Your first attempt and review give separate feedback; you can see which counting patterns still need practice.

valuesStart.restsLesson: Read rests and include their durations
valuesStart.longBody: A $t(glossary:noteValue_one) describes how long a sound lasts relative to other sounds. One $t(glossary:notes.whole_one) equals two $t(glossary:notes.half_other) or four $t(glossary:notes.quarter_other). A $t(glossary:notes.half_one) therefore lasts twice as long as a $t(glossary:notes.quarter_one). The 4/4 at the start of the notation means that one $t(glossary:measure_one) contains four $t(glossary:notes.quarter_other). The upper 4 counts the units; the lower 4 names the $t(glossary:notes.quarter_one) as the unit. In these examples, each $t(glossary:notes.quarter_one) takes one steady beat: count 1–2–3–4. The longest note starts on 1 and lasts through the end of 4; the two half-length notes start on 1 and 3. All examples take the same total time. The time in seconds depends on tempo. You do not need to name the pitch here.
valuesStart.shapesBody: The $t(glossary:notehead_one) is the oval symbol. A $t(glossary:notes.whole_one) has an unfilled head without a $t(glossary:stem_one); a $t(glossary:notes.half_one) has an unfilled head with a stem. A $t(glossary:notes.quarter_one) has a filled head and stem without a $t(glossary:flag_one). A $t(glossary:notes.eighth_one) has one flag and a $t(glossary:notes.sixteenth_one) has two. Adjacent short notes may use $t(glossary:beam_other) instead: one beam replaces one flag, two replace two flags. Stem direction does not change duration. The example contains a $t(glossary:notes.half_one), a $t(glossary:notes.quarter_one), a $t(glossary:notes.eighth_one) and two $t(glossary:notes.sixteenth_other). Recognition questions show individual symbols.
valuesStart.shortTitle: There is time between beats too
valuesStart.shortBody: Two $t(glossary:notes.eighth_other) last as long as one $t(glossary:notes.quarter_one); so do four $t(glossary:notes.sixteenth_other). Their lengths are therefore one half and one quarter of that beat unit. One $t(glossary:notes.whole_one) divides into eight $t(glossary:notes.eighth_other) or sixteen $t(glossary:notes.sixteenth_other). Count 1-and–2-and–3-and–4-and with the first example. The second has four equal sounds per beat. Shortest to longest means: $t(glossary:notes.sixteenth_one), $t(glossary:notes.eighth_one), $t(glossary:notes.quarter_one), $t(glossary:notes.half_one), $t(glossary:notes.whole_one). All values in this unit are undotted.
valuesStart.longRestsBody: A $t(glossary:rest_one) means that this voice stays silent for its duration. The $t(glossary:pulse) continues. A $t(glossary:rests.whole_one) is a rectangle hanging below a line; a $t(glossary:rests.half_one) sits on a line. On the staff, the first hangs from the fourth line from the bottom; the second sits on the third. Individual question symbols retain a short reference line. Here in four-four time their durations are four and two beats. The hanging rectangle can also indicate a complete silent bar regardless of time signature; here we use that function only in four-four. The first audio example is completely silent; keep counting four beats.
valuesStart.shortRestsBody: The $t(glossary:rests.quarter_one) is a vertical jagged symbol with a curved lower end. The $t(glossary:rests.eighth_one) has one hook on a slanted stroke; the $t(glossary:rests.sixteenth_one) has two. Their durations match the corresponding note values: one beat, half a beat and a quarter of a beat when a $t(glossary:notes.quarter_one) is the beat. The example contains all three rest symbols, each followed by a sound of equal length. Listen to the gaps and follow the symbols in order. Rests are not joined by beams.
valuesStart.silenceBody: Four beat units can contain both sound and silence. In the first example a note sounds on 1 and 3, while 2 and 4 are silent. Keep counting all four beats evenly. In the second, the sound lasts two beats and silence lasts two beats. Both fill the same total time. In matching questions, connect each rest name to its duration as a fraction of a $t(glossary:notes.whole_one). The fractions 1/2, 1/4, 1/8 and 1/16 mean one half, one quarter, one eighth and one sixteenth of that reference duration.
valuesStart.capacityTitle: These bars hold four beat units
valuesStart.capacityBody: A $t(glossary:measure_one) groups a defined span of time. This unit uses only 4/4: the upper 4 requires four units; the lower 4 names the $t(glossary:notes.quarter_one) as the unit. Notes and rests together must equal exactly four of these units. In the example, the $t(glossary:notes.half_one) contributes two, the $t(glossary:rests.quarter_one) one, and the final note one: 2 + 1 + 1 = 4. Other time signatures follow in the next unit; their accents come later. Here you calculate duration without needing to know all time signatures.
valuesStart.barlinesBody: A $t(glossary:barline_one) is the thin vertical line between adjacent $t(glossary:measure_other). It creates neither sound nor silence and adds no duration. After it, counting starts again at 1. A $t(glossary:finalBarline_one) consists of a thin line and a thicker line, marking the end of a piece or complete section. The example shows two complete four-four bars: a single dividing line between them and an ending at the right. A boundary does not change the duration of the note written before it.
valuesStart.completeBody: Read the numbered question symbols from left to right, continuing on the next row if they wrap. The question mark is the final missing value. Convert all visible notes and rests to beat units, add them, then subtract from four. In the first example, the first three symbols total 2 + 1 + 1/2 = 3 1/2; the final $t(glossary:notes.eighth_one) fills the missing half-beat. In the second, 2 + 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 leaves one quarter of a beat for the final $t(glossary:rests.sixteenth_one). Check whether the question asks for a note or a rest. Both overfilling and underfilling are incorrect.
valuesStart.shapesCaption: One half-length, one quarter-length, one eighth-length and two sixteenth-length notes
valuesStart.halfRestCaption: Two silent beats, then a sound lasting two beats
valuesStart.silenceCaption: Sounds on 1 and 3, silence on 2 and 4
valuesStart.silentHalfCaption: A $t(glossary:notes.half_one) and a $t(glossary:rests.half_one) total four beat units
valuesStart.barlinesCaption: Two $t(glossary:measure_other), one boundary and one ending
valuesStart.articleTitle: Note values, rests and complete bars

simpleMeterStart.articleTitle: Simple metres: count in and follow note onsets
simpleMeterStart.twoBody: The upper number of the time signature gives the number of crotchet values here; the lower 4 names the crotchet as the unit. A 2/4 $t(glossary:measure_one) lasts two crotchets: count 1–2, then start again at 1 in the next $t(glossary:measure_one). Two quavers together occupy the same time as one crotchet. In the second example you hear two note onsets during beat 1 and one on beat 2. Pitch does not matter for this rhythm task.
simpleMeterStart.threeBody: A 3/4 $t(glossary:measure_one) contains three crotchet values. Count 1–2–3, then begin the next $t(glossary:measure_one) at 1. The 1 helps you locate the start; this notation does not prescribe an extra accent. Compare the length of a 3/4 $t(glossary:measure_one) with 2/4 when both use the same tempo.
simpleMeterStart.fourBody: A 4/4 $t(glossary:measure_one) holds four crotchet values. Count 1–2–3–4 and begin again at 1 in the next $t(glossary:measure_one). The lower 4 still names the crotchet value, not the tempo. In the example, each crotchet begins on a beat and lasts until the next. Read the time signature before counting individual notes.
simpleMeterStart.countBody: Before each tapping task, you hear one complete $t(glossary:measure_one) as a count-in. Count two steady beats in 2/4, three in 3/4 or four in 4/4. Count along silently and begin only on the next 1, when recording starts. The example plays the written $t(glossary:measure_one); the count-in sounds only when you start a tapping task. Then tap note onsets only.
simpleMeterStart.pickupTitle: An upbeat is shorter than a full $t(glossary:measure_one)
simpleMeterStart.pickupBody: An upbeat precedes the first bar line and does not fill the time signature. In the 3/4 example only one crotchet value appears before that line; in the 4/4 example two quavers also make only one crotchet value. The next $t(glossary:measure_one) shows the full length in each case. Add the values before the first bar line and compare them with three or four crotchet values. The upbeat question checks this notation; tapping tasks still start after a full count-in $t(glossary:measure_one).
simpleMeterStart.completeTitle: A full first $t(glossary:measure_one) is no upbeat
simpleMeterStart.completeBody: All beats can already be present before the first visible bar line. Here three crotchets add up to exactly three crotchet values. The first $t(glossary:measure_one) is complete, so the bar line alone does not prove an upbeat. Check the duration of the first group of notes and use the following complete $t(glossary:measure_one) as a comparison.
simpleMeterStart.eighthBody: Two quavers fill one crotchet beat. Count a quaver pair as “1 and” and tap at both note onsets. The next crotchet begins on 2. In the 4/4 example there are still four steady crotchet beats, even though the second beat divides into two notes. Tap at the start of a note, never continuously while it lasts.
simpleMeterStart.restsBody: A crotchet rest occupies a whole crotchet beat; a quaver rest occupies half of one. Keep counting steadily through silence. In the 3/4 example tap on 1 and 3, but not 2. In the 2/4 example the first half of 1 is silent; the quaver begins on “and”, the crotchet on 2. An extra tap during a rest counts as an error.
simpleMeterStart.readBody: Read the time signature first, then work through the values from left to right. Two quavers occupy one crotchet value; rests occupy time without a note onset. Count through the full count-in $t(glossary:measure_one), then tap only the onsets of visible notes. At 72 or 96 beats per minute the underlying beat stays steady and the second quaver of each pair falls halfway between beats. Practise one $t(glossary:measure_one) slowly and inspect missing or extra taps in the feedback.
simpleMeterStart.twoEighthCaption: Two quavers on 1 and, then a crotchet on 2.
simpleMeterStart.countCaption: Three beats in 3/4; the next 1 follows the $t(glossary:measure_one).
simpleMeterStart.pickupCaption: Upbeat: one crotchet before the first bar line in 3/4.
simpleMeterStart.pickupEighthCaption: Upbeat: two quavers make one crotchet value before the first bar line in 4/4.
simpleMeterStart.completeCaption: No upbeat: the first 3/4 $t(glossary:measure_one) is complete.
simpleMeterStart.eighthFourCaption: Four beats with two quavers on beat 2.
simpleMeterStart.restsEighthCaption: First half of the beat silent, note on “and”, note on 2.
simpleMeterStart.readCaption: Quaver onsets on 1 and, then a rest, then notes on 3 and 4.
simpleMeterStart.readThreeCaption: Silence first, two quavers on 2 and, then a note on 3.
simpleMeterStart.countInLesson: Count in and spot an upbeat
simpleMeterStart.countTwoCaption: Two beats in 2/4; then the next 1 begins.

intervalSizeStart.numbersLesson: Count intervals from unison to octave
intervalSizeStart.directionLesson: Ascending, descending or the same pitch
intervalSizeStart.motionLesson: Recognise repeated notes, steps and leaps
intervalSizeStart.articleTitle: Read interval number, direction and motion
intervalSizeStart.countTitle: Include both end positions in the interval number
intervalSizeStart.countBody: An $t(glossary:interval_one) describes the distance between two pitches. Its number counts letter-name positions, including the start and destination. From E4 to G4, count E–F–G: 1–2–3, so it is a $t(glossary:third_one). Each next line or space takes you to the next letter-name position. Count positions, not the number of drawn notes. Both notes here have the same duration; duration does not determine the interval number.
intervalSizeStart.smallBody: Two identical natural pitches form a $t(glossary:unison_one) with the number 1. You see two successive notes, but both occupy the same letter-name position. The next position makes a $t(glossary:second_one), for example E–F: 1–2. With one position between them, you get a $t(glossary:third_one), such as E–F–G: 1–2–3. The starting note always counts as 1.
intervalSizeStart.largeBody: Four counted positions make a $t(glossary:fourth_one), five a $t(glossary:fifth_one), six a $t(glossary:sixth_one), seven a $t(glossary:seventh_one) and eight an $t(glossary:octave_one). From E4 to A4, count E–F–G–A: four positions. From E4 to E5, follow E–F–G–A–B–C–D–E: eight positions. After B comes C in the next octave register. The number alone does not tell you whether an interval is minor, major or perfect; these quality names follow in the next unit.
intervalSizeStart.upBody: Read the two notes from left to right. If the second notehead sits higher on the stave, pitch moves upward. Here G4 rises to B4. Stem direction does not determine this; compare the noteheads. You can then count the interval number: G–A–B occupies three positions.
intervalSizeStart.downBody: In a descending pattern, the second notehead sits lower. Here B4 moves to G4: count B–A–G, again three positions. A third stays a third when you reverse the order. Direction and number answer different questions. Start at the first written note with 1 and count toward the second.
intervalSizeStart.sameBody: If both natural notes occupy the same line or space and octave register, pitch stays the same. Select “Same pitch” for the direction. Here A4 appears twice. The interval number is 1. There are no accidentals in this unit; altered notes on the same letter-name position come later.
intervalSizeStart.repeatBody: A $t(glossary:noteRepetition_one) repeats the same pitch. Both noteheads occupy the same position and the interval is a unison. In the sound example, you hear two separate onsets of F4. The second note is a new onset even though pitch stays the same. The interval number remains 1.
intervalSizeStart.stepTitle: A step moves to the next letter-name position
intervalSizeStart.stepBody: A $t(glossary:melodicStep_one) connects immediately adjacent letter-name positions and forms a second. No letter-name position is skipped between the two noteheads. E–F is a semitone and F–G is a tone, yet both patterns are steps with interval number 2. This applies when ascending or descending. A step here is therefore not a fixed number of piano keys.
intervalSizeStart.leapBody: A $t(glossary:melodicLeap_one) leaves at least one letter-name position between the start and destination. In this unit, a third or larger is a leap: G–B skips A; E–B skips F, G and A. Larger leaps can reach an octave. Find the direction first, then count positions: 1 means repeated note, 2 means step, and 3 through 8 mean leap. Note duration does not change this classification.
intervalSizeStart.countCaption: E4–G4: E–F–G, three positions, a third.
intervalSizeStart.primeCaption: G4–G4: the same position, unison with number 1.
intervalSizeStart.secondCaption: E4–F4: two adjacent positions, a second.
intervalSizeStart.upCaption: G4–B4: the second notehead is higher.
intervalSizeStart.downCaption: B4–G4: the second notehead is lower.
intervalSizeStart.repeatCaption: F4–F4: two onsets of the same pitch.
intervalSizeStart.halfStepCaption: E4–F4: a step with a semitone distance.
intervalSizeStart.wholeStepCaption: F4–G4: a step with a tone distance.

firstQualityStart.perfectLesson: Check perfect fourths, fifths and octaves
firstQualityStart.articleTitle: Semitone distances and first interval qualities
firstQualityStart.transitionsBody: A $t(glossary:semitone_one) is the distance between immediately adjacent piano keys, regardless of colour. For sounding distance, the starting key counts as 0; each move to the next key adds 1. E–F has one move, so the distance is one semitone. Two identical pitches have no move: distance 0. This differs from interval-number counting, where the starting note counts as 1. In the exercises, the notation and marked piano keys show the same two pitches.
firstQualityStart.blackKeysTitle: Include black keys in the count
firstQualityStart.blackKeysBody: Count every immediately adjacent key, including black keys. F–F-sharp–G has two moves, giving two semitones. G–G-sharp–A–A-sharp–B has four moves, giving four semitones. Do not count only white keys or the number of marked keys. E to F and B to C have no intervening black key; one move is enough there. The keys between the marked endpoints help you count.
firstQualityStart.largerTitle: Count larger distances in the same way
firstQualityStart.largerBody: E4 to A4 spans five semitones; E4 to E5 spans twelve. Continue counting adjacent-key moves for a larger distance. In descending tasks, count toward the lower pitch; the answer is still a positive distance. The lower and upper marked keys are the two endpoints. Note values determine duration, not semitone distance.
firstQualityStart.thirdNumberTitle: A third always has the number 3
firstQualityStart.thirdNumberBody: Before naming a $t(glossary:third_one) more precisely, check its number: three letter-name positions including start and destination. A–B–C forms a third, as do E–F–G and F–G–A. Now add a second property: distance in semitones. Thirds on natural notes, as used in this unit, span three or four semitones. The extra name is the $t(glossary:intervalQuality_one). Number and quality together make the full interval name.
firstQualityStart.minorBody: A minor third combines interval number 3 with three semitones. For E4–G4, the letter-name positions E–F–G number three. On the keyboard, the moves E–F–F-sharp–G also give three semitones, starting at 0. The answer is “minor third”. A descending minor third still spans three semitones; read its direction from the notation. Note duration does not determine quality.
firstQualityStart.majorBody: A major third still has number 3 but spans four semitones. F–G–A occupies three letter-name positions; F–F-sharp–G–G-sharp–A spans four key moves. G–B is also a major third of four semitones. Two thirds therefore need not look differently spaced on the stave. After counting letter-name positions, check sounding distance. This unit uses natural notes in the treble clef only.
firstQualityStart.perfectBody: A perfect fourth combines number 4 with five semitones; a perfect fifth combines number 5 with seven. E–F–G–A occupies four letter-name positions: E4–A4 is a perfect fourth spanning five semitones. E–F–G–A–B occupies five: E4–B4 is a perfect fifth spanning seven. “Perfect” is the quality name for these intervals. Both number and semitone distance must fit; the number of positions alone is not enough.
firstQualityStart.octaveBody: A perfect $t(glossary:octave_one) repeats a letter name in the next octave register. E–F–G–A–B–C–D–E occupies eight letter-name positions and spans twelve semitones. E4–E5 is therefore a perfect octave. Reversing the order keeps the twelve-semitone distance and makes the pattern descending. Distinguish equal letter names in different registers from a repeated pitch with distance 0.
firstQualityStart.tritoneBody: A $t(glossary:tritone_one) spans three tones, or six semitones; strictly, this means F–B. F–B has interval number 4 but six semitones instead of five; it is not a perfect fourth. B to F in the next register has number 5 but six semitones instead of seven; it is not a perfect fifth. B–F spans the same number of $t(glossary:semitone_other) as F–B and is often also called a tritone. Answer “No” for both when checking perfect intervals. The two notations share a semitone distance but have different interval numbers. Their other quality names come later.
firstQualityStart.zeroCaption: G4–G4: the same key again, 0 moves.
firstQualityStart.minorCaption: E4–G4: number 3 and 3 semitones, minor third.
firstQualityStart.majorCaption: F4–A4: number 3 and 4 semitones, major third.
firstQualityStart.majorOtherCaption: G4–B4: also a major third with 4 semitones.
firstQualityStart.fourthCaption: E4–A4: number 4 and 5 semitones, perfect fourth.
firstQualityStart.fifthCaption: E4–B4: number 5 and 7 semitones, perfect fifth.
firstQualityStart.octaveCaption: E4–E5: number 8 and 12 semitones, perfect octave.
firstQualityStart.tritoneFourthCaption: F4–B4: number 4 and 6 semitones, not a perfect fourth.
firstQualityStart.tritoneFifthCaption: B4–F5: number 5 and 6 semitones, not a perfect fifth.

auralRhythmStart.card1Body: The $t(glossary:pulse) provides a regular sense of time. Listen to the higher starting sounds and the evenly spaced clicks that follow. All beats between two beginnings belong to one group; the next beginning belongs to the next group. You can quietly count or move along. Here, clicks deliberately make the pulse clear.
auralRhythmStart.card1Example1: Two beats per group, heard twice.
auralRhythmStart.card1Example2: Three beats per group, heard twice.
auralRhythmStart.card2Body: The $t(glossary:rhythm_one) can contain several starts within a pulse beat and silent passages. The pulse continues as a reference. Listen first to the steady sequence, then to the example with shorter sounds. A new note start is not automatically a new pulse beat. This unit begins with simple crotchet and quaver patterns.
auralRhythmStart.card2Example2: Two short sounds share the first crotchet beat.
auralRhythmStart.card3Title: Do not count the next beginning twice
auralRhythmStart.card3Body: When listening to two groups, start counting at the higher click with 1. In a four-beat group, 2, 3 and 4 follow. The next higher click begins again at 1. Loudness and pitch help identify the beginning here; this does not imply that every musical beginning must sound higher.
auralRhythmStart.card4Title: Compare two rhythms using the same rule
auralRhythmStart.card4Body: You hear example A, a short separating gap and example B. Here, “same” means the same note starts, durations and rests at the same tempo. Both examples use the same piano pitch so that pitch does not distract from rhythm. Listen to both in full and start again from the beginning when replaying.
auralRhythmStart.card4Example1: A: the second beat is divided.
auralRhythmStart.card4Example2: B: the same starts and durations as A.
auralRhythmStart.card5Body: Two examples can have the same number of note starts and still have different rhythms. Compare which beat contains the short sounds. In the first example, the first beat is divided; in the second, the second beat is divided. Both bars have the same total length. Simply counting notes is therefore insufficient.
auralRhythmStart.card5Example1: A: two quavers at the beginning.
auralRhythmStart.card5Example2: B: two quavers after the first crotchet.
auralRhythmStart.card6Title: Rests are part of the comparison
auralRhythmStart.card6Body: A $t(glossary:rest_one) is a notated silent span. It does not end the bar. Keep listening until the next note start and maintain the pulse internally. Replacing a note with a rest changes the audible rhythm even when the total bar length stays the same. The separating gap between A and B is not part of either example bar.
auralRhythmStart.card6Example1: A crotchet rest on the third beat.
auralRhythmStart.card6Example2: A crotchet sounds at that point instead.
auralRhythmStart.card7Title: Match a heard rhythm to notation
auralRhythmStart.card7Body: In the selection question, you hear exactly one complete bar. The three numbered scores show different rhythms on the same pitch. Read their beginnings and find the first point where they differ. Then match the heard starts, durations and rests. A score number does not indicate whether it is correct.
auralRhythmStart.card7Example1: The third crotchet beat consists of two quavers.
auralRhythmStart.card8Body: A $t(glossary:notes.quarter_one) lasts one pulse beat here; two $t(glossary:notes.eighth_other) divide it equally. A sound can continue without a new start. Listen to both starts and duration. All scores form the same complete four-four bar; their events must add up to the bar length.
auralRhythmStart.card9Title: Find silence in the matching score
auralRhythmStart.card9Body: When you hear a short gap, look for the corresponding rest in the score. Do not confuse a note ending without a new start with an additional note. The examples begin with a note and contain no accidentals or dots. You can replay freely; unavailable audio is recorded as skipped listening work.
auralRhythmStart.card9Example1: A quaver rest follows the first crotchet.
auralRhythmStart.lesson3: Match a heard rhythm to its score

auralPitchStart.articleTitle: Pitch direction, melodies and first listening intervals
auralPitchStart.card1Body: Compare the second sound with the first. For “higher”, sounding pitch increases. The second sound need not be louder or longer. Listen to the pitches in sequence; the question asks for no note names and requires no absolute pitch. Direction will later be linked to interval names.
auralPitchStart.card2Body: For “lower”, sounding pitch decreases. Do not equate a quieter sound with a lower pitch. In the example, A4 is followed by F4; the second lies lower. The score stays hidden before checking in listening questions so that the answer is based on hearing.
auralPitchStart.card3Body: A repeated pitch has two separate starts at the same pitch. It is not one long sound. For “same pitch”, compare height rather than the number of starts. Both sounds use the same piano timbre in these questions, keeping the focus on direction and repetition.
auralPitchStart.card4Body: For melody comparisons, you hear four pitches in A and then four in B. “Same” means the same sounding pitches in the same order with the same durations. A similar contour or transposed sequence is not “same” here. Both examples stay short and use natural notes so you can follow each pitch mentally.
auralPitchStart.card5Body: Two melodies can begin and end on the same pitch while a middle pitch differs. Compare each position in order. In these examples, only the second pitch changes; durations remain the same. One difference is enough for “different”. You do not need to name every note.
auralPitchStart.card5Example1: A has G4 in the second position.
auralPitchStart.card6Body: Hear the first melody as a short unit, then compare the beginning, middle and end of the second. Tempo and timbre stay the same within a question; pitch and timing are the assessed properties. The gap helps orientation and is not part of the melody. Replaying supports learning without creating a new question.
auralPitchStart.card6Example1: Beginning G4, middle E4–F4, ending G4.
auralPitchStart.card7Title: Hear ascending minor and major thirds
auralPitchStart.card7Body: A minor third spans three semitones; a major third spans four. Both are $t(glossary:third_other); by ear, their sounding distances differ. Here, the starting pitch is followed by the higher destination. Compare the two original examples without relying on song openings as fixed mnemonics. The introductory score provides a check.
auralPitchStart.card8Title: Hear ascending perfect fourths and fifths
auralPitchStart.card8Body: A perfect fourth spans five semitones; a perfect fifth spans seven. These questions play pitches in ascending sequence rather than simultaneously. Compare the distance from the first pitch. The example can start in a different register; the interval name depends on the relationship, not an absolute note name.
auralPitchStart.card9Body: Finally, minor third, major third, perfect fourth and perfect fifth are offered together. Hear the starting pitch and then the distance. All questions remain ascending and use natural notes. Further qualities, descending listening intervals and longer melodies belong to the next level. An error review uses a new sound rather than only rearranged buttons.
auralPitchStart.card9Example1: G4–B4: a major third from a different starting pitch.
auralPitchStart.lesson1: Hear higher, lower and repeated pitches
auralPitchStart.lesson3: Hear ascending thirds, fourths and fifths

historySourcesStart.articleTitle: Sound sources, documents and musical context
historySourcesStart.card1Body: A $t(glossary:voice_one) is produced in singing by vibrating vocal folds. An $t(glossary:instrument_one) uses a vibrating string, membrane or air column, for example. Electronic devices can generate audio signals. These describe production rather than mutually exclusive labels for an entire recording: one performance can combine several sound sources.
historySourcesStart.card1Example1: The model plays piano pitches and does not reproduce a singing voice. Original piano teaching model.
historySourcesStart.card2Title: A recording is a playback medium
historySourcesStart.card2Body: A $t(glossary:recording_one) stores sound for later playback. It can contain voices, instruments and electronic sounds together. A loudspeaker reproduces the stored signal; it alone does not establish how the original sound was produced. Distinguish production from playback. Our sound examples are original piano teaching models rather than historical performances.
historySourcesStart.card2Example1: The written score is played as a piano model here. Original piano teaching model.
historySourcesStart.card3Body: “Singing with piano accompaniment” identifies a voice and an instrument. “A recording of it” adds the medium without replacing those sources. A choir consists of several singers; a choir recording is both vocal sound and stored playback. You should not guess human voices or instrument identities from our piano models. The questions ask about unambiguous descriptions of these terms.
historySourcesStart.card3Example1: A single written melody does not by itself establish choir forces. Original piano teaching model.
historySourcesStart.card4Title: Distinguish a score from a performance
historySourcesStart.card4Body: A $t(glossary:scoreSource_one) uses symbols to specify pitches, durations and further instructions. It does not itself sound. A performance realises those instructions through decisions about tempo, timbre and shaping. Our displayed teaching score and playback intentionally match exactly; historical sources require separate consideration of edition, transmission and interpretation.
historySourcesStart.card4Example1: Written instructions and their sounding realisation. Original piano teaching model.
historySourcesStart.card5Body: A recording lets you hear particular starts, sound shapes and interpretative choices. It does not automatically prove identical notation or a correct label. Editing, splicing and playback technology can affect the result. Check recording date, performers and provenance separately. This teaching model demonstrates only its own played score.
historySourcesStart.card5Example1: An audible rest is an observation about this model. Original piano teaching model.
historySourcesStart.card6Body: A $t(glossary:report_one) describes an event from one perspective. A $t(glossary:programmeSource_one) announces a work, performers, place and date, for example. An announcement alone does not prove that everything occurred; a report can be mistaken. Compare sources and distinguish their claims. Fictional teaching information is explicitly labelled and does not replace historical evidence.
historySourcesStart.card6Example1: Fictional programme: “Piano teaching model, town hall, 2026”. Original piano teaching model.
historySourcesStart.card7Body: The $t(glossary:place_one) asks where a performance happened. Sources may name a church, concert hall or private room. A short piano sound alone does not establish a performance venue. The example’s fictional programme says “town hall”: that is place information, not a listening observation. Real history requires checkable provenance and sources.
historySourcesStart.card7Example1: Fictional teaching information: venue town hall. Original piano teaching model.
historySourcesStart.card8Title: Date composition, performance and recording separately
historySourcesStart.card8Body: The $t(glossary:time_one) asks when a particular event occurred. A work’s composition, a later performance and a still later recording can have different dates. Identify which date a source refers to. “2026” in the fictional teaching programme is an event date; it does not date a historical composition. A familiar sound style does not replace this evidence.
historySourcesStart.card8Example1: Fictional teaching information: event date 2026. Original piano teaching model.
historySourcesStart.card9Body: The $t(glossary:occasion_one) names the event, such as a wedding or benefit concert. $t(glossary:author) asks who wrote the music or report. Performers, composers and reporters can be different people. In the fictional example, “benefit concert” is the occasion. These categories help read sources purposefully and identify unsupported guesses.
historySourcesStart.card9Example1: Fictional teaching information: occasion benefit concert. Original piano teaching model.
historySourcesStart.lesson3: Identify place, time and occasion in a source

historyOverviewStart.articleTitle: Periods, performing forces and supported listening observations
historyOverviewStart.card1Title: A broad sequence of European periods
historyOverviewStart.card1Body: This introduction covers European art music rather than the entire history of world music. The conventional broad sequence is Middle Ages, Renaissance, Baroque, Classical period, Romantic period and music since 1900. It supports orientation in time and does not rank styles as better. Ordering questions ask for this sequence. The piano model is not a historical style sample and cannot be dated from it.
historyOverviewStart.card1Example1: A simple-sounding melody does not establish a medieval date. Original piano teaching model.
historyOverviewStart.card2Title: Approximate dates rather than rigid boundaries
historyOverviewStart.card2Body: For learning orientation, we use roughly 500–1400 for the Middle Ages, 1400–1600 for the Renaissance and 1600–1750 for the Baroque. For the Classical period, roughly 1750–1820; for Romanticism, mainly the nineteenth century. Boundaries vary by region and topic; Classical and Romantic periods overlap. The sequence is an overview, not an automatic way to date music.
historyOverviewStart.card2Example1: A piano model alone provides no evidence for a period. Original piano teaching model.
historyOverviewStart.card3Body: “Music since 1900” groups the twentieth and twenty-first centuries here. It is not a single style. Earlier music also continues to be performed and newly recorded. Composition date and the date of a heard recording remain separate questions. Period terms help organise information; detailed work histories and further musical traditions are explored later.
historyOverviewStart.card3Example1: A present-day teaching model can use the same pitches as earlier music. Original piano teaching model.
historyOverviewStart.card4Title: Genre names a kind of work
historyOverviewStart.card4Body: A $t(glossary:genre_one) describes a kind of work. In this introduction, an opera combines mostly sung music with staged action; a symphony is typically a multi-movement orchestral composition. These short descriptions do not replace the history of their varied forms. Genre does not establish the specific event where a work was performed. A short melody alone does not reliably identify an opera or symphony.
historyOverviewStart.card4Example1: Four notes do not establish a genre. Original piano teaching model.
historyOverviewStart.card5Body: The $t(glossary:performingForces_one) describes participating voices and instruments. A choir consists of several singers; an orchestra of several instrumental performers. A string quartet normally uses two violins, viola and cello. Children’s, men’s and women’s choirs are descriptions of forces; a single pitch does not establish these forces. Genre and forces answer different questions.
historyOverviewStart.card5Example1: Two piano pitches are not a recording of a choir or string quartet. Original piano teaching model.
historyOverviewStart.card6Title: Occasion and function are different questions
historyOverviewStart.card6Body: Occasion names the specific event, such as a wedding ceremony. $t(glossary:function_one) asks what purpose music served there: dancing, worship or focused listening, for example. The same work can serve different purposes in different contexts. Performing forces are therefore neither a function nor automatically a genre. Read carefully which question is described in an exercise.
historyOverviewStart.card6Example1: Sound alone establishes neither a wedding nor a dance function. Original piano teaching model.
historyOverviewStart.card7Title: Call only what is heard an observation
historyOverviewStart.card7Body: A $t(glossary:observation_one) describes directly checkable sound. “Two pitches sound together” can be heard in the example. “The piece originated in a church in 1750” includes date and place claims for which the example alone provides no evidence. Our models contain either pitches sounding only in sequence or at least one joint start of two pitches.
historyOverviewStart.card7Example1: One pitch, silence, then another pitch. Original piano teaching model.
historyOverviewStart.card7Example2: Two pitches begin together. Original piano teaching model.
historyOverviewStart.card8Body: $t(glossary:sourceInformation_one) may give place, date or authorship. An $t(glossary:inference_one) combines observations and checked information into an informed conclusion. Neither sound similarity nor an unchecked label alone establishes certainty. Identify the source of a statement and distinguish it from what you directly heard. The exercise asks for the directly audible statement about the original model.
historyOverviewStart.card8Example1: The pitches and rest are audible; no historical date is given. Original piano teaching model.
historyOverviewStart.card9Body: When evidence is missing or contradictory, $t(glossary:uncertainty) is an accurate description. You do not need to guess a venue or period. Check whether a statement is supported by hearing or an appropriate source. Starts and simultaneous pitches can be checked in the original piano model; historical provenance is not claimed. This keeps observation precise and history connected to sources.
historyOverviewStart.card9Example1: A joint start does not establish historical provenance. Original piano teaching model.

clefsStart.articleTitle: Bass clef, grand stave and octave names
clefsStart.anchorBody: The two dots of the $t(glossary:bassClef_one) surround the fourth line from the bottom. That line is f, or F3 scientifically. This is why it is also called the F clef. Count lines from the bottom; the same position has a different name in another clef.
clefsStart.ladderTitle: Step by step from c to b
clefsStart.ladderBody: Moving from a line to the next space is one letter-name step. In the $t(glossary:bassClef_one), c/C3 occupies the second space from the bottom. Above it come d, e, f, g, a, b. The third, fourth and fifth lines hold d, f and a; e and g lie between them, and b lies just above the top line. Use reference notes and count in either direction.
clefsStart.middleBody: After b/B3, c¹/C4 starts the next $t(glossary:octaveRegister_one). This middle C occupies the first $t(glossary:ledgerLine_one) above the bass stave. The short line belongs to the note. c and c¹ share their letter name but are an octave apart. Include the register in the final four questions.
clefsStart.pairBody: The $t(glossary:grandStaff_one) connects an upper stave in the $t(glossary:trebleClef_one) with a lower stave in the $t(glossary:bassClef_one). The connection groups them together; each clef retains its own pitch mapping. Two staves do not imply exactly two voices or a compulsory division between hands. Here only one contains a note; the other has a whole-bar rest.
clefsStart.sharedBody: c¹/C4 occupies the first $t(glossary:ledgerLine_one) below the upper stave in the $t(glossary:trebleClef_one). The same pitch lies on the first above the lower stave in the $t(glossary:bassClef_one). The examples show these spellings separately: both sound the same and mark the same key. Their available pitch ranges overlap; a note on the lower stave is not automatically lower than every note on the upper one.
clefsStart.findTitle: From stave to the right key
clefsStart.findBody: Read the clef of the stave containing the note first. Then identify its letter name and $t(glossary:octaveRegister_one) before choosing a key. Here you practise a/A3 through e¹/E4, with the keyboard fixed to that range. b/B3 is the white key immediately left of c¹/C4. A rest on the other stave adds no second target pitch.
clefsStart.helmBody: The $t(glossary:helmholtzNotation) uses case and superscripts: C is great C (C2), c is small c (C3), c¹ is one-line c (C4), and c² is two-line c (C5). The same register marking applies to all seven letter names: c–b, then c¹–b¹. Our exercises start at C3; the card also shows C2 for comparison.
clefsStart.scienceBody: In $t(glossary:scientificNotation), a number follows the international uppercase letter: C3–B3, then C4–B4. Middle C is C4. The number changes at C, not at A. Switching naming systems preserves the pitch. Translate Helmholtz to scientific notation in the first half, then in the opposite direction.
clefsStart.lettersBody: This lesson always uses international scientific names: German h = B3 and German h¹ = B4. German B would be a lowered H, international B♭; it is absent from these natural-note tasks. Check both the letter-name system and the register when translating. The right letter in the wrong octave is an incorrect answer.
clefsStart.sharedExample1: c¹ = C4 in the treble clef
clefsStart.sharedExample2: c¹ = C4 in the bass clef: the same key
clefsStart.scienceExample1: B3 → C4: the number increases at C
clefsStart.lettersExample1: German h, international b; scientifically B3

levelTwoSpelling.articleTitle: Accidentals, enharmonic spelling and note writing
levelTwoSpelling.scopeBody: An $t(glossary:accidental_one) before a note applies to later notes of the same letter in the same octave until the next bar line. In this example F-sharp repeats in the same bar without a second sharp. Read clef, bar and register together.
levelTwoSpelling.scopeCaption: F-sharp twice; the second sharp is not printed again
levelTwoSpelling.resetTitle: A bar line resets the state
levelTwoSpelling.resetBody: At the $t(glossary:barline_one), an individual accidental’s scope ends. The $t(glossary:keySignature_one) applies again. With no key signature, F-sharp in the first bar becomes F in the next. A tie specially continues the same pitch; the rhythm unit covers that case.
levelTwoSpelling.resetCaption: F-sharp before the bar line, F afterwards
levelTwoSpelling.naturalBody: A $t(glossary:natural_one) cancels the alteration previously in force for this letter in this register. In our reading model, an accidental on F4 does not automatically affect F5. Key signatures apply to their letter names in every octave. These tasks use single accidentals.
levelTwoSpelling.naturalCaption: F-sharp, cancelled F, F-sharp, and F in the next octave
levelTwoSpelling.enharmonicTitle: C-sharp and D-flat share a key
levelTwoSpelling.enharmonicBody: With $t(glossary:enharmonic), differently written pitches can sound alike. C-sharp raises C; D-flat lowers D. On an equal-tempered piano both reach the same key. Their written letters remain different and matter for intervals and chords.
levelTwoSpelling.enharmonicCaption: C-sharp and D-flat: same key, different letter positions
levelTwoSpelling.edgesTitle: Even without an intervening black key
levelTwoSpelling.edgesBody: E–F and B–C already span one $t(glossary:semitone_one). E-sharp therefore sounds like F, and B-sharp like the next C. An alteration belongs to the written letter, rather than a key colour. B-sharp can have a different scientific octave number from its equivalent C.
levelTwoSpelling.spellingTitle: Sound equivalence does not preserve notation
levelTwoSpelling.spellingBody: Finding a key requires the correct sounding pitch. Writing a note also requires its letter, alteration and octave. D-flat therefore does not correctly spell a requested C-sharp, even though they sound alike. Check whether each task asks about sound or spelling.
levelTwoSpelling.spellingCaption: Two sounding equivalents followed by natural C
levelTwoSpelling.writeBody: When writing, place the $t(glossary:notehead_one) on the correct letter-name position, then choose the single accidental. The task names a full pitch: C4 is a different register from C3. Check the clef before moving the notehead.
levelTwoSpelling.writeCaption: D4 and D-sharp4 keep the same letter position
levelTwoSpelling.bassTitle: The bass clef keeps its mapping
levelTwoSpelling.bassBody: In the $t(glossary:bassClef_one), C4 occupies the first ledger line above the stave. C-sharp retains that notehead position and adds a sharp. In treble clef this pitch lies below the stave. Sound follows pitch; position follows clef.
levelTwoSpelling.bassCaption: C4 and C-sharp4 in bass clef
levelTwoSpelling.checkBody: Check letter name, accidental and register in that order. Writing controls change these properties separately. The first evaluation locks the answer; an error review uses a new pitch. Enharmonic replacements count as errors in these writing tasks.
levelTwoSpelling.checkCaption: B-flat3 and B3 in the same register

levelTwoDottedTied.dotBody: A dot extends a note value by half its original value. A dotted crotchet equals crotchet plus quaver: 1 + 1/2 = 3/2 crotchet values. This is a duration, rather than a new meter. This unit uses exactly one dot.
levelTwoDottedTied.dotCaption: Dotted crotchet plus quaver equals two crotchets
levelTwoDottedTied.eighthBody: A dotted quaver equals quaver plus semiquaver. Together with another semiquaver it fills one crotchet value. The two onsets divide that span unequally: three sixteenths to one. First count equal small subdivisions.
levelTwoDottedTied.fractionBody: A dotted half lasts three crotchet values. A dotted quaver instead lasts three crotchets of one crotchet value. A number needs a reference unit. These tasks explicitly bar duration in crotchet values.
levelTwoDottedTied.tieBody: A $t(glossary:tie) connects consecutive notes of the same written pitch. The second note has no new onset; durations are added. Connecting different pitches is not a tie. A phrase or slur marking has a different function.
levelTwoDottedTied.tieCaption: Two tied crotchets: one sound across two beats
levelTwoDottedTied.chainBody: Three or more identical notes can form a tie chain. Read through the first note without a further tie. Rests do not belong to that chain. Here G has one onset and lasts three crotchet values; the following rest is silent.
levelTwoDottedTied.compareTitle: Compare a dot and a tie
levelTwoDottedTied.compareBody: A dotted crotchet and a tied crotchet plus quaver have the same total duration. The second spelling makes a subdivision clearer. Compare duration while retaining the written structure. Here each of the two pitches lasts one and a half crotchet values.
levelTwoDottedTied.compareCaption: Dotted G; A tied for the same duration
levelTwoDottedTied.crossbarBody: A $t(glossary:barline_one) does not end a tie. The pitch continues into the next bar without a new onset there. Its alteration also carries through the tie. Add the note values on both sides to find total duration.
levelTwoDottedTied.crossbarCaption: F-sharp starts before the bar line and continues afterwards
levelTwoDottedTied.syncopationBody: In this simple $t(glossary:syncopation_one), a pitch starts between beats and continues across the following beat, bridging a normally stronger position. A short offbeat quaver alone does not meet this task’s criterion. Listen for the uninterrupted duration.
levelTwoDottedTied.syncopationCaption: Onset on the second quaver, held across the next crotchet beat
levelTwoDottedTied.countBody: Keep counting beats evenly even when no new note starts. A tie adds no onset. Later tapping tasks count actual onsets only. Compare the syncopation with this sequence whose note starts fall on beats.

levelTwoSubdivision.threeTitle: Three in the time of two
levelTwoSubdivision.threeBody: A $t(glossary:triplet_one) divides the time of two equal notes into three equal parts. Three triplet quavers together last as long as two ordinary quavers: one crotchet. The number 3 labels the group rather than the meter.
levelTwoSubdivision.threeCaption: Three triplet quavers within one crotchet
levelTwoSubdivision.equalBody: The three triplet parts have equal duration. This is neither a dotted long-short rhythm nor an unequal swing instruction. Count three evenly spaced syllables per crotchet beat. The task checks all three actual onsets.
levelTwoSubdivision.equalCaption: Two crotchet beats, each divided into three
levelTwoSubdivision.tapBody: Before tapping, hear a complete count-in bar. Then enter each written note onset. Each three-quaver triplet fills exactly one beat. The fourth onset begins the next group of three; avoid adding a pause between groups.
levelTwoSubdivision.tapCaption: Nine onsets within three crotchet beats
levelTwoSubdivision.simpleBody: Simple 3/4 has three crotchet beats. Each normally divides into two quavers. Six quaver notes fill the bar, grouped 2 + 2 + 2. The meter and beam groups show that organization.
levelTwoSubdivision.compoundBody: Compound 6/8 normally groups its six quavers as 3 + 3. Its two beats each have the value of a dotted crotchet. The numerator 6 does not imply six ordinary beats here. Read the quavers as subdivisions within the two groups.
levelTwoSubdivision.sameTotalBody: At the same quaver duration, 3/4 and 6/8 have equal total length. Their usual grouping differs: three pairs versus two triples. The denominator alone does not always describe the musical beat. These tasks ask about beat count and beat value together.
levelTwoSubdivision.groupBody: The $t(glossary:beam_other) group quavers by the two beats in 6/8. Group one starts on quaver 1; group two starts on quaver 4. Count each beat with three even subdivisions. Actual onsets may occupy only some of those positions.
levelTwoSubdivision.groupCaption: Quarter plus quaver, then quaver plus crotchet
levelTwoSubdivision.restsBody: A rest has the same duration as the corresponding note value. It places the following note on its proper subdivision. Do not tap a rest, but continue counting internally. These tasks use the dotted crotchet as the count-in beat.
levelTwoSubdivision.distinguishBody: Three ordinary quavers already form one beat in 6/8, so no triplet number is required. Three quavers under a 3 within a crotchet beat are instead a triplet. Both have three parts but different reference units; always check the meter.
levelTwoSubdivision.distinguishCaption: Ordinary quavers in 6/8, without a triplet number

levelTwoQualitiesBuild.numberBody: The $t(glossary:intervalQuality_one) requires both letter-name distance and semitone distance. Include both endpoints when counting the number. C–E is a third; C–F is a fourth. Then check sounding steps. A semitone count alone does not determine an interval’s full spelling.
levelTwoQualitiesBuild.familiesBody: Unison, fourth, fifth and octave belong to the perfect classes. Second, third, sixth and seventh initially distinguish minor and major. Augmented and diminished alterations are possible in both families. This stage covers simple intervals through the octave.
levelTwoQualitiesBuild.familiesCaption: Perfect fourth: four letter names, five semitones
levelTwoQualitiesBuild.qualitiesTitle: Altering a pitch preserves its letter
levelTwoQualitiesBuild.qualitiesBody: An accidental changes sounding distance without changing letter position. C–E is major and C–E-flat minor; both remain thirds. C–F-sharp is an augmented fourth. Comparing with a perfect or major reference helps naming, but does not replace counting.
levelTwoQualitiesBuild.buildNumberBody: To build a major third from C, count C as 1, D as 2 and E as 3. This fixes the target letter E. Then determine its alteration. The writing task preserves the starting pitch and asks for the complete second pitch.
levelTwoQualitiesBuild.buildQualityBody: A minor third from D needs F: three semitones. A major third from D needs F-sharp: four. Both use the letter F. Add an accidental when the requested quality requires it, and retain the correct octave.
levelTwoQualitiesBuild.buildCheckBody: Check the counted letters first, then the semitone count. An enharmonically equivalent key with the wrong letter does not meet the writing task. The exact written pitch, including alteration and octave, matters here. The display uses German or English note names.
levelTwoQualitiesBuild.tritoneBody: C–F-sharp and C–G-flat sound alike on an equal-tempered piano. The first spans four letters and is an augmented fourth; the second spans five and is a diminished fifth. Both are tritone distances. Visual tasks can distinguish these spellings; purely aural tasks cannot.
levelTwoQualitiesBuild.thirdFourthTitle: Four semitones can also be ambiguous
levelTwoQualitiesBuild.thirdFourthBody: C–E is a major third. C–F-flat sounds the same but is a diminished fourth. The flat lowers a perfect fourth by one semitone. Its number remains a fourth because the letter is F. Sounding distance alone therefore cannot supply a reliable full interval name.
levelTwoQualitiesBuild.contextBody: Key and later chord function can explain a spelling choice. In these tasks, spelling is already supplied: count precisely what is written. Do not first replace notes with more convenient enharmonic names. Use sound afterwards as a check.

levelTwoInversion.articleTitle: Interval inversion, direction and octave relationships
levelTwoInversion.invertTitle: Move an endpoint by an octave
levelTwoInversion.invertBody: To invert a simple interval, move its lower endpoint up an octave or its upper endpoint down an octave. The endpoints exchange order within the octave. C–E becomes E–C in the next register: a sixth, rather than a third simply played downwards.
levelTwoInversion.invertCaption: C–E, followed by its inversion E–C
levelTwoInversion.nineBody: Simple interval inversion numbers add to 9: second and seventh, third and sixth, fourth and fifth. Unison and octave form the edge case. Include both endpoints again. The octave displacement is part of the inversion.
levelTwoInversion.qualityBody: Perfect remains perfect; minor and major exchange. Augmented becomes diminished and diminished becomes augmented. A major third therefore inverts to a minor sixth. Adding the numbers is not enough: check quality as well.
levelTwoInversion.qualityCaption: Minor sixth as inversion of a major third
levelTwoInversion.descendingTitle: Count from the upper starting pitch
levelTwoInversion.descendingBody: When building downwards, preserve the named starting pitch. For a descending third from E, count E as 1, D as 2 and C as 3. Direction changes the letter sequence. This differs from the octave displacement used for inversion.
levelTwoInversion.downQualityBody: A descending major third from C reaches A-flat, four semitones lower. A is only three semitones lower, a minor third. First count descending letters, then sounding distance. Crossing below C also changes the register.
levelTwoInversion.downCheckBody: A descending perfect fifth from G reaches C. G, F, E, D, C are five counted letters; sounding distance is seven semitones downwards. It remains a perfect fifth rather than becoming a fourth because of its direction.
levelTwoInversion.compoundBody: A ninth is octave plus second; a tenth is octave plus third. Adding an octave raises the interval number by 7, not 8, because the shared endpoint counts once. Sounding distance increases by twelve semitones.
levelTwoInversion.compoundCaption: Major ninth: octave plus major second
levelTwoInversion.reduceBody: A major tenth reduces by one octave to a major third. Subtract 7 from the number while preserving quality. A minor ninth reduces to a minor second. This maps the interval class; the actual upper register remains visible in the score.
levelTwoInversion.reduceCaption: Major tenth maps to major third
levelTwoInversion.octavesBody: A perfect double octave has number 15. Removing one octave leaves a simple octave. Reduction stops within the simple interval range from unison through octave; a simple octave is therefore not reduced further to unison. Read the question carefully.

levelTwoMajor.patternTitle: Whole and half in a fixed order
levelTwoMajor.patternBody: A major scale follows 2–2–1–2–2–2–1 semitones. Its half steps lie between degrees 3–4 and 7–8. This pattern stays the same when the tonic changes. Read adjacent pitches rather than counting visible accidentals.
levelTwoMajor.patternCaption: C major with half steps E–F and B–C
levelTwoMajor.lettersBody: A seven-note major scale uses its seven letter names in order. The quaver pitch repeats the tonic one octave higher. Accidentals adjust sounding distances while retaining the letter sequence. G major therefore uses F-sharp rather than G-flat.
levelTwoMajor.lettersCaption: G major: one sharp on F
levelTwoMajor.transposeTitle: Apply the pattern from a new tonic
levelTwoMajor.transposeBody: Starting from F, natural notes would put a tone between degrees 3 and 4. B-flat lowers degree four to create the required semitone. German calls this lowered B-natural B; internationally it is B♭. The major pattern works in flat keys too.
levelTwoMajor.buildBody: The starting pitch stays fixed when writing a scale. Supply the next seven pitches through the octave. Choose each letter before its alteration. A correct sounding key with the wrong letter does not satisfy this spelling task.
levelTwoMajor.buildCaption: D major uses F-sharp and C-sharp
levelTwoMajor.threeBody: Writing tasks use major keys with zero through three sharps or flats: C, G, D, A and F, B-flat, E-flat. Octave is part of every answer. The next C after B starts the next scientific octave number; check this boundary carefully.
levelTwoMajor.threeCaption: A major: F-sharp, C-sharp and G-sharp
levelTwoMajor.checkBody: Check the letter sequence and then all seven sounding distances. A correctly written major scale needs both. Afterwards, hear the complete scale; its ending repeats the tonic in a higher register. An error review uses a different scale source.
levelTwoMajor.tonicBody: The $t(glossary:tonic_one) is the tonic of the key. In G major, G is degree one rather than C. The example’s starting pitch explicitly establishes that mapping. Degrees are positions within a scale rather than absolute piano-key numbers.
levelTwoMajor.tonicCaption: G is degree 1; B is degree 3
levelTwoMajor.degreesBody: Assign degrees 1 through 7 to the ascending scale notes. The octave endpoint is the tonic again. An accidental changes a degree’s sounding pitch rather than its position number. These tasks name a full pitch for you to locate in the scale shown.
levelTwoMajor.degreesCaption: B-flat is degree 4 in F major
levelTwoMajor.relationBody: C is the tonic of C major but degree four in G major. Its role depends on the scale. Answer degree questions after checking the starting pitch and major pattern. This prepares you to build diatonic triads later.
levelTwoMajor.relationCaption: C as degree four in G major

levelTwoMinor.naturalBody: Natural minor follows 2–1–2–2–1–2–2 semitones. Degree three is a minor third above the tonic. A natural minor uses natural notes from A through A; other tonics need alterations. The letter sequence remains ordered.
levelTwoMinor.thirdTitle: The minor third as a feature
levelTwoMinor.thirdBody: Major and natural minor differ in degree three: C major uses E and C minor E-flat. Natural minor also lowers degrees six and seven relative to same-tonic major. One isolated note does not automatically establish a real piece’s key; here you explicitly hear and write complete scales.
levelTwoMinor.thirdCaption: C minor with E-flat, A-flat and B-flat
levelTwoMinor.minorSignatureBody: Natural minor preserves the pitches of its key signature. E minor has F-sharp; G minor has B-flat and E-flat. The next key unit studies these signatures systematically. Here check written pitches against the natural-minor pattern.
levelTwoMinor.seventhBody: In this scale model, harmonic minor raises natural minor’s seventh degree by one semitone. In A minor, G becomes G-sharp, leaving a semitone to A. The key signature remains that of A natural minor.
levelTwoMinor.augmentedSecondBody: F and G-sharp in A harmonic minor are three semitones apart. Their adjacent letters make an augmented second rather than a minor third. This scale still needs every letter in order. Sounding distance must not replace spelling.
levelTwoMinor.raiseTitle: A raised degree is relative to its existing pitch
levelTwoMinor.raiseBody: Raising does not always mean adding a sharp. Natural C minor has B-flat as degree seven; harmonic minor changes it to B-natural. Compare the natural starting form with the target pitch. The task evaluates the resulting exact spelling.
levelTwoMinor.melodicUpTitle: Raise degrees six and seven ascending
levelTwoMinor.melodicUpBody: Classical melodic minor ascending raises degrees six and seven of natural minor by one semitone each. In A minor these become F-sharp and G-sharp. The pattern is 2–1–2–2–2–2–1. The minor third above the tonic remains.
levelTwoMinor.melodicDownBody: In this classical teaching model, melodic minor descending returns to natural-minor degrees. Descending from A gives G, F, E, D, C, B and A. A recognition task must not offer this as a sounding alternative to descending natural minor.
levelTwoMinor.melodicDownCaption: A melodic minor descending: natural degrees
levelTwoMinor.conventionBody: Real melodies use raised or natural degrees according to musical context rather than always following direction. Jazz teaching may retain ascending melodic minor’s raised degrees when descending too. These tasks explicitly use the classical scale convention to make both directions unambiguous.

levelTwoKeys.articleTitle: Signatures, circle of fifths and related keys
levelTwoKeys.signatureTitle: A signature applies in every octave
levelTwoKeys.signatureBody: A $t(glossary:keySignature_one) applies to its letter names in every octave until changed. A local accidental can alter it within a bar. These tasks explicitly supply major or minor, because the same signature belongs to two relative keys.
levelTwoKeys.signatureCaption: G major: the signature raises every F
levelTwoKeys.sharpsBody: The first three sharps belong to F, C and G, producing G, D and A major from C major. Each added sharp retains earlier ones; any three letter positions will not do. The final sharp is one semitone below the major tonic.
levelTwoKeys.flatsBody: The first three flats belong to B, E and A: B-flat, E-flat and A-flat. Their major keys are F, B-flat and E-flat. German distinguishes H and B; internationally these are B and B♭. Check both actual signs and the naming language.
levelTwoKeys.flatsCaption: E-flat major with B-flat, E-flat and A-flat
levelTwoKeys.fifthsBody: On the $t(glossary:circleOfFifths), C and G are neighbours, as are G and D. An ascending fifth moves one signature step towards sharps. It can first remove a flat, as F major to C major does. This lesson’s tasks stay in major.
levelTwoKeys.backwardsBody: A descending fifth from C reaches F. This moves one circle step towards flats. From D major, the same step reaches G major and removes one sharp. The task states direction and mode; do not also change major to minor.
